Will you not remember?﴾ ﴿To Him is your return﴾, your return. ﴿All together﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial state. ﴿The promise of Allah is true﴾: truthful, with no failing in it. It is in the accusative as an absolute object, meaning Allah promised a promise, a true promise, so He brought it as true. It was also said: it is in the accusative of emphasis. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *wa'd Allahi haqq* (the promise of Allah is true) as an independent statement. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it﴾ [Yunus: 4], meaning He brings them into existence, then makes them die, then brings them back to life. The common readers read *innahu* (indeed) with a kasra on the *alif*, as a new sentence. Abu Ja'far read *annahu* with a fatha, meaning "because He" and "that He". [In Zad al-Masir (4/7) there is an addition: 'Aisha, Abu Razin, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah, and al-A'mash read it with a fatha. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it with a kasra, it is a new sentence; whoever reads it with a fatha, the meaning is: "To Him is your return."] This is like the saying of the poet:

*Is it true, servants of Allah, that I will not visit*
*Buthaynah, or that the Pleiades will meet her watcher?* [In Lisan: "meeting" instead of "visiting". Lisan al-'Arab: 1/425.]

﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾: that He may reward them, with justice, meaning with fairness. Then He said, beginning anew: ﴿And those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water﴾ [Yunus: 4]: water that is hot, whose heat has reached its extreme, *hamim*, which means *mahmum* (heated), an *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*. Among the Arabs, every heated, boiling liquid is *hamim*. Al-Marqash said:

*Every day for her there is a perfuming, in which is incense burned and scalding water.* [*Al-kaba'*: a kind of wood used for fumigation. The verse is in Lisan al-'Arab: 5/107.]

﴿And a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾.

Makkan. It has 10,889 letters, about 2,500 words (more than one word is uncounted), and 109 verses.

Hamid ibn Ahmad, Sa'id ibn Muhammad, and Muhammad ibn al-Qasim narrated to us. They said: Muhammad ibn Mutar informed us: Ibrahim ibn Shurayk, Ahmad ibn Yunus, Salam ibn Sulaym, and Harun ibn Kathir, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Abu Umamah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat Yunus will be given a reward and good deeds equal to the number of those who believed in Yunus and denied him, and equal to the number of those who drowned with Pharaoh."

[76] The Messenger of Allah spoke the truth.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*Alif-Lam-Ra* (الر) is recited with *tafkhim* (emphatic pronunciation), with *imalah* (inclination of the vowel), and with a pronunciation between the two. All of these are sound and eloquent dialects.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: it means "I am Allah, the All-Seeing." It was also said: "I am the Lord; there is no lord but Me." 'Ikrimah, al-A'mash, and al-Sha'bi said: the letters *Alif-Lam-Ra* and *Ha-Mim-Nun* are the separated letters of *al-Rahman* (the Most Gracious); when they are joined, it becomes *al-Rahman*. Qatadah said: it is one of the names of the Qur'an. Abu Rawq said: it is the opening of the surah. It was also said: it is the oaths of Allah. It was also said: it is an oath, as if he said: "By Allah, indeed these are the verses of the Book."

Mujahid and Qatadah said: it refers to the Torah, the Gospel, and the sacred scriptures, and *tilka* (those) is a reference to a feminine absent thing.

Others said: it refers to the Qur'an, and this is more correct, because He did not specify the earlier scriptures before mentioning it, and because the *Hakim* (the Wise) is the one who sent the Qur'an. Its proof is His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾ [Hud: 1], and similar verses. On this interpretation, *tilka* means *hadhihi* (these). The discussion of this question has already passed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-Hakim* (the Wise): the one who is judged by what is lawful and unlawful, by the prescribed limits, and by the rulings.

Muqatil said: *al-Muhkam* means that which is distinguished from falsehood; there is no lie in it and no contradiction. It is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, like the saying of al-A'mash in his qasidah:

*And a resolute command that comes to kings, decisive;*
*I have said it so that it may be said: who has said it?*

It was also said: *Hakim* is the one who judges, *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il*, because He sent down: ﴿the Book with truth, that it may judge between the people concerning that over which they differ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. It was also said: it means "the one judged," *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*.

Al-Hasan said: He judged in it with ﴿justice and beneficence and giving to kinsfolk﴾ [al-Nahl: 90], and He judged in it with the prohibition of ﴿immorality and wrongdoing and oppression﴾, and He judged in it with Paradise for whoever obeys Him and with the Fire for whoever disobeys Him.

'Ata' said: *Hakim* is He who decides by what He wills concerning provisions and terms of life.

﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them﴾ [Yunus: 2]. Ibn 'Abbas said: when Allah sent Muhammad as a messenger, the disbelievers denied it and said: "Allah is too great for His messenger to be a human like Muhammad." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, and the *alif* is for rebuke, *'ajaban* (a wonder), ﴿that We revealed﴾. *An* (that) is in the nominative position, and *awhayna* (We revealed) is its relative clause, the meaning being: "Is it a wonder for the people that We have revealed to a man from among them, Muhammad?" In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: *'ajib* (a wonder), in the nominative as the subject of *kana*, and *an* is in the accusative position as its predicate. ﴿That warn the people﴾: *an* is in the accusative position by the implied omission of the preposition, and likewise the second *an*.

﴿And give good tidings to those who have believed that they will have a sure standing with their Lord﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: a good reward for what they sent forward of their deeds. Al-Dahhak said: a true reward. Mujahid said: the righteous deeds. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: happiness was decreed for them in the first remembrance.

*Qadam sidq* (a sure standing): Zayd ibn Aslam said: Muhammad (ﷺ) is their intercessor. Yaman said: their faith. 'Ata' said: a station of truth, without cessation or distress, enduring bliss and eternity, an eternity without death. Al-Hasan said: a righteous deed they sent forward, for which they were rewarded. Al-A'mash said: a precedence of truth. Abu Hatim said: a dwelling of truth, like His saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance﴾ [al-Isra': 80]. 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya said: *qadam sidq*. Concerning His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101]. Al-Zajjaj said: a lofty rank. It was also said: it is their resurrection, and Allah's placing this nation first in resurrection on the Day of Judgment. Its explanation is his (ﷺ) saying: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Judgment." It was also said: it is Allah's promise to them. *Qadam* (standing) is like *naqs* (decrease) and *qabd* (grip). The *qadam* was attributed to *sidq* (truth), and this is [a qualifier], as one says *masjid al-jami'* (the congregational mosque) and *haqq al-yaqin* (the truth of certainty).

Ibn al-A'rabi said: *qadam* is precedence in nobility.

Al-'Ajjaj said:

*The sons of al-'Awwam slipped away from the family of al-Hakam,*
*and left the kingship to a king of precedence.*

That is, one who is preceding. [Lisan al-'Arab: 1/103, where it reads: "and they despised the kingship of a king of precedence."]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Kisa'i said: every one who precedes in good or evil is, in the language of the Arabs, *qadam*. It is said: "So-and-so has *qadam* in Islam," and "He has a *qadam sidq* (true standing) with me," and "*qadam sau'* (evil standing)." It is feminine; one says *qadam hasanah* (good standing) and *qadam salihah* (righteous standing). Hassan ibn Thabit said:

*For us is the highest precedence toward You, and those who follow us are behind our first in obedience to Allah.*

Dhu al-Rummah said:

*For you is a precedence that people do not deny,*
*along with an ancient lineage that overflowed the sea.*

Another said:

*The precedence of the wicked held them back, and their lineages were mentioned*
*from silver and from the mint.*

That is, what the wicked put forward for them.

﴿The disbelievers said: Indeed, this is clearly a magician﴾ [Yunus: 2]. The exegetes said: the Qur'an. The people of Kufa read *lasahir* (a magician), meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne, arranging the matter﴾ [Yunus: 3]. Mujahid said: He decrees it alone. ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾, His command. ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾: the One who did these things, ﴿your Lord﴾, there is no lord for you other than Him. ﴿So worship Him. Will you not remember?﴾ ﴿To Him is your return﴾, your return. ﴿All together﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial state. ﴿The promise of Allah is true﴾: truthful, with no failing in it. It is in the accusative as an absolute object, meaning Allah promised a promise, a true promise, so He brought it as true. It was also said: it is in the accusative of emphasis. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *wa'd Allahi haqq* (the promise of Allah is true) as an independent statement. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it﴾ [Yunus: 4], meaning He brings them into existence, then makes them die, then brings them back to life. The common readers read *innahu* (indeed) with a kasra on the *alif*, as a new sentence. Abu Ja'far read *annahu* with a fatha, meaning "because He" and "that He". [In Zad al-Masir (4/7) there is an addition: 'Aisha, Abu Razin, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah, and al-A'mash read it with a fatha. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it with a kasra, it is a new sentence; whoever reads it with a fatha, the meaning is: "To Him is your return."] This is like the saying of the poet:

*Is it true, servants of Allah, that I will not visit*
*Buthaynah, or that the Pleiades will meet her watcher?* [In Lisan: "meeting" instead of "visiting". Lisan al-'Arab: 1/425.]

﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾: that He may reward them, with justice, meaning with fairness. Then He said, beginning anew: ﴿And those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water﴾ [Yunus: 4]: water that is hot, whose heat has reached its extreme, *hamim*, which means *mahmum* (heated), an *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*. Among the Arabs, every heated, boiling liquid is *hamim*. Al-Marqash said:

*Every day for her there is a perfuming, in which is incense burned and scalding water.* [*Al-kaba'*: a kind of wood used for fumigation. The verse is in Lisan al-'Arab: 5/107.]

﴿And a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾.

He it is who made the sun a radiance by day and the moon a light by night. Al-Kalbi said: their faces shine upon the people of the seven heavens, and their backs upon the people of the seven earths.

[Most readers recited ﴿ḍiyā'an﴾ with a single hamza.] It is narrated from Ibn Kathir: ﴿ḍi'ā'an﴾ with a hamza on the ya', but there is no basis for it, because its ya' was originally a fatha-vowelled waw, the middle radical of the verb. Its root was ḍiwā'; it became sakin and was made a ya', as in ṣiyām and qiyām. ﴿Wa-qaddarahu manāzila﴾: he measured it, meaning he prepared it and arranged for it stations it would neither exceed nor fall short of.

It was said: qaddara is of the type that takes two objects, yet it did not say qaddarahumā. The sun and the moon have been mentioned, and there are two possibilities. The first is that the pronoun refers to the moon alone, through the crescents by which the passing of months and years is known, not the sun. The second is that one of the two has been mentioned and the other omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [9:62]. This issue has already been discussed. ﴿Li-ta'lamū ʿadada al-sinīn﴾: so that you may know the number of years, their entry and their passing; ﴿wa-al-ḥisāb﴾: and the reckoning, meaning the reckoning of the months, the days and the hours. ﴿Mā khalaqa Allāh dhālika﴾: Allah did not create that, such as the distinction, the creation and the measuring, except with truth. Had the aforementioned entities [i.e., the sun and the moon] been meant, it would have said: "those." ﴿Illā bi-al-ḥaqq﴾: He did not create it in vain, but to manifest His craftsmanship and to indicate His power and wisdom. ﴿Wa-li-tujzā kull nafs bi-mā kasabat﴾: and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned. This is the truth. ﴿Yufaṣṣilu al-āyāt﴾: He makes the signs distinct, clarifying them ﴿li-qawmin yaʿlamūn﴾: for a people who know.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim recited ﴿yufaṣṣilu﴾ with a ya', and Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Ḥātim preferred this because of His preceding words ﴿mā khalaqa Allāh﴾ and His following words ﴿wa-mā khalaqa Allāh﴾, so it follows them. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ recited it with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the ṣad, and a raf' on the tā' of ﴿al-āyāt﴾, in the passive voice. The rest recited it with a nun, in the plural of majesty.

﴿Inna fī ikhtilāf al-layl wa-al-nahār wa-mā khalaqa Allāh fī al-samāwāt wa-al-arḍ la-āyātin li-qawmin yattaqūn﴾: Indeed in the alternation of night and day, and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, there are signs for a people who fear Allah, meaning who are certain, and so know and affirm.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the people of Mecca said, "Bring us a sign so that we may believe in you." So Allah revealed this verse.

﴿Inna alladhīna lā yarjūna liqāʾanā﴾: Indeed those who do not hope for meeting Us, meaning they do not fear Our punishment and do not hope for Our reward. Rajāʾ can mean dread and fear. ﴿Wa-raḍū bi-al-ḥayāt al-dunyā﴾: and are content with the life of this world, choosing it as their abode. ﴿Wa-iṭma'annū bihā﴾: and feel at rest in it, settling into it.

Qatada said concerning this verse: if you wish, you will see a man of this world who rejoices for it, grieves for it, is pleased for it and is angry for it.

﴿Wa-alladhīna hum ʿan āyātinā﴾: and those who are heedless of Our signs, meaning Our proofs, ﴿ghāfilūn﴾: they take no lesson. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Our signs" means Muḥammad and the Qur'an. ﴿Ghāfilūn﴾: they turn away, abandon, and deny. ﴿Ulāʾika mā'wāhum al-nār bi-mā kānū yaksibūn﴾: those, their abode is the Fire because of what they earned, namely disbelief and denial. ﴿Inna alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt yahdīhim rabbuhum bi-īmānihim﴾: indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith. There is an implied ellipsis here: their Lord will guide them by their faith to a place ﴿tajrī min taḥtihimu al-anhār﴾: beneath them rivers flow.

Abu Rawq said: ﴿yahdīhim rabbuhum bi-īmānihim﴾ means "to Paradise." ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿yahdīhim﴾ means He will guide them, reward them and recompense them. It was also said: He will deliver them.

Mujāhid and Muqātil said: ﴿yahdīhim﴾ means He will guide them with light on the path (ṣirāṭ) to Paradise; He will make for them a light by which they walk.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the believer comes out of his grave, his deed takes for him a form, a good form and a good tiding. He says to him: 'Who are you? By Allah, I see you as a man of truth.' He says: 'I am your deed.' So it becomes for him a light and a guide to Paradise. When the disbeliever comes out of his grave, his deed takes for him an evil form and a foul smell. He says: 'Who are you? By Allah, I see you as a man of evil.' He says: 'I am your deed.' So it takes him away until it brings him into the Fire."

It was said: the meaning of the verse is: by their faith their Lord guides them to His religion, that is, by their affirmation He guides them. ﴿Tajrī min taḥtihimu al-anhār﴾: it is not meant that the rivers flow beneath them while they are above them, for the rivers of Paradise flow without trenches (ukhādīd). Rather the meaning is that they flow beside them, before them, and under their command, as in His saying: ﴿Your Lord has placed a stream beneath you﴾ [19:24]. It is well known that He did not place the stream beneath her while she was seated upon it; rather He meant before her. Likewise His saying, reporting of Pharaoh: ﴿Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flow beneath me?﴾ [43:51], or "beneath my command."

﴿Fī jannāt al-naʿīm﴾: in gardens of bliss. ﴿Daʿwāhum﴾: their call, meaning their saying and speech, ﴿fīhā subḥānaka Allāhumma﴾: therein: "Glory be to You, O Allah."

Ṭalḥa ibn ʿAbd Allah said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about "Subḥān Allāh," and he said: "It is the declaration of Allah's transcendence above every imperfection." Ibn al-Kawwā asked ʿAlī about this, and he said: "It is a word which Allah has approved for Himself."

The exegetes said: [this is a blessing; a knowledge is shown to them, and the servants (khadam) are visible at the meal]. When they desire some food or drink, they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah." Then, at that moment, they are brought what they desire on a table. When they have finished eating and drinking, they praise Allah for what He has given them. That is His saying: ﴿wa-ākhiru daʿwāhum an al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi rabbi al-ʿālamīn﴾: and their last call is: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." It does not mean the last speech they utter, but the one before it.

al-Ḥasan said: it reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he recited this verse, said: "The people of Paradise are inspired to praise and glorify, just as they are inspired to breathe." That is His saying: ﴿daʿwāhum fīhā subḥānaka Allāhumma wa-taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾: their call therein is "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein is peace, in Paradise; they greet one another with peace, and the angels come to them from their Lord with peace.

Ibn Kaysan said: they begin their speech with monotheism and end it with praise.

The common readers recited ﴿anni al-ḥamdu li-Allāh﴾ with the light form and a raf', while Bilāl ibn Abī Burda and Ibn Muḥayṣin recited ﴿anna﴾ in the heavy form with al-ḥamda in the accusative.

﴿Wa-law yuʿajjilu Allāh li-al-nās al-sharr﴾: and if Allah were to hasten evil for people. There is an ellipsis here; its meaning is: ﴿wa-law yuʿajjilu Allāh li-al-nās...﴾, the verse [continuing], their going astray in polytheism. ﴿Istiʿjālahum bi-al-ijāba fī al-khayr﴾: as their haste for the answer to their requests for good. ﴿La-quḍiya ilayhim ajaluhum﴾: their term would have been decreed for them, that is, their destruction would have been decreed, and they would all have died.

Mujāhid said: it is the saying of a person to his child, his property, when he is angry: "O Allah, destroy him! O Allah, do not bless him in it, and curse him!" A man may make such a prayer against himself, his child, his family or his property, with what he would dislike to be answered.

Shahr ibn Ḥawshab: I read in some books that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to the two angels charged with recording: "Do not write anything against My servant in a state of his distress."

The common readers recited ﴿la-quḍiya ilayhim ājāluhum﴾ with a ḍamma on the qāf and the lām, as a passive verb with a nominative subject. ʿAwf, ʿĪsā, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb recited it with a fatḥa on the qāf and the lām. al-Aʿmash recited: ﴿la-quḍīnā﴾, and so it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah.

It was said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith when he said: ﴿Allāhumma in kāna hādhā huwa al-ḥaqq min ʿindika fa-amṭir ʿalaynā ḥijāratan min al-samāʾ﴾: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky" [8:32]. This is supported by His saying: ﴿fa-nadharu alladhīna lā yarjūna liqāʾanā﴾: so We leave those who do not hope for meeting Us, who do not fear resurrection and reckoning and do not hope for reward, ﴿fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn﴾: wandering blindly in their rebellion.

﴿Wa-idhā massa al-insān al-ḍurr﴾: and when harm touches man, meaning hardship and distress, ﴿daʿānā li-janbihi﴾: he calls upon Us, lying on his side, ﴿aw qāʿidan aw qāʾiman﴾: or sitting or standing. He means all his states, because a person does not go beyond one of these conditions. ﴿Falammā kashafnā ʿanhu ḍurrahu﴾: but when We remove and relieve him of his harm, ﴿marra kaʾan lam yadʿunā ilā ḍurrin massah﴾: he goes on as though he had never called upon Us to remove a harm that had touched him, meaning he continues in his former way. It was said: when harm touches him, he forgets what he was in of hardship and affliction, and abandons thanks and supplication. al-Akhfash said: ﴿ka-an lam yadʿunā﴾ and ﴿ka-an lam yalbathū﴾ and similar, where ka-anna is the heavy form and the emphatic: "as if he had not called upon Us." ﴿Kadhālika zuyyina lil-musrifīn﴾: thus it was made attractive to the wasteful, meaning: just as the call in time of affliction was made attractive to this man, and turning away in time of ease, so too the wasteful were made to see as fine their striving in disbelief and disobedience. ﴿Mā kānū yaʿmalūn﴾: what they did of disbelief and disobedience. Wastefulness (isrāf) may be of the self. In one reading: he wasted himself, making it a worshipper of an idol, and wasted his property by making it [unprofitable, without good]. The meaning is: they were excessive in their worship and excessive in their expenditure.

﴿Wa-laqad ahlaknā al-qurūn min qablikum﴾: We destroyed generations before you, meaning the past nations. Ibn ʿAbbas said: between the two horns [generations] were twenty-eight years. ﴿Lammā ẓalamū﴾: when they did wrong, that is, they associated partners with Allah. ﴿Wa-jāʾathum rusuluhum bi-al-bayyināt﴾: their messengers came to them with clear proofs, ﴿wa-mā kānū li-yuʾminū﴾: but they would not believe. ﴿Kadhālika﴾: thus, as We destroyed them for their disbelief and their denial of their messengers, ﴿najzī﴾: We destroy ﴿al-qawm al-mujrimīn﴾: the wicked people, the polytheists, whose denial of Muḥammad (ﷺ) warns the disbelievers of Mecca of the punishment of the earlier, denying nations.

﴿Thumma jaʿalnākum khalāʾifa fī al-arḍ min baʿdihim﴾: then We made you successors in the earth after them, meaning after the generations We destroyed, ﴿li-nanẓura﴾: so that We may see, that is, so that We may know, ﴿kayfa taʿmalūn﴾: how you act, though He knows them best.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed this world is green and sweet, and Allah has made you its successors in it, so He will look at how you act."

Qatada: it has been related to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Allah has spoken the truth; our Lord did not make us successors except that He might look at our deeds. So show Allah good deeds, by night and by day, in secret and in public."

Thābit al-Bunānī narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Layla that ʿAwf ibn Mālik said to Abu Bakr: "I saw in a dream, as one who sleeps sees, that something was lowered to me from the sky, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took hold of it, and then it was returned, and Abu Bakr took hold of it; then people measured around the pulpit, and ʿUmar was found to be three cubits more than the pulpit." ʿUmar said: "Leave us from your dream; we have no need of it." When ʿUmar became caliph, he said: "Tell me your dream, O ʿAwf." He said: "Do you have any need of my dream?" He said: "Did you not forbid me?" He said: "Woe to you! I disliked that you should announce to the caliph of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) his own death." Then he related the dream to him, until when he reached the measuring of the people around the pulpit with these three cubits, ʿUmar said: "As for the first, you will indeed be caliph. As for the second, he will not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of Allah. As for the third, he will be a martyr." Qatada said concerning this verse: if you wish, you will see a man of this world who rejoices for it, grieves for it, is pleased for it and is angry for it.

The exegetes said: [this is a blessing; a knowledge is shown to them, and the servants (khadam) are visible at the meal]. When they desire some food or drink, they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah." Then, at that moment, they are brought what they desire on a table. When they have finished eating and drinking, they praise Allah for what He has given them. That is His saying: ﴿wa-ākhiru daʿwāhum an al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi rabbi al-ʿālamīn﴾: and their last call is: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." It does not mean the last speech they utter, but the one before it.

al-Ḥasan said: it reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he recited this verse, said: "The people of Paradise are inspired to praise and glorify, just as they are inspired to breathe." That is His saying: ﴿daʿwāhum fīhā subḥānaka Allāhumma wa-taḥiyyatuhum fīhā salām﴾: their call therein is "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein is peace, in Paradise; they greet one another with peace, and the angels come to them from their Lord with peace.

Ibn Kaysan said: they begin their speech with monotheism and end it with praise.

The common readers recited ﴿anni al-ḥamdu li-Allāh﴾ with the light form and a raf', while Bilāl ibn Abī Burda and Ibn Muḥayṣin recited ﴿anna﴾ in the heavy form with al-ḥamda in the accusative.

There is an ellipsis here; its meaning is: ﴿wa-law yuʿajjilu Allāh li-al-nās...﴾, the verse [continuing], their going astray in polytheism. ﴿Istiʿjālahum bi-al-ijāba fī al-khayr﴾: as their haste for the answer to their requests for good. ﴿La-quḍiya ilayhim ajaluhum﴾: their term would have been decreed for them, that is, their destruction would have been decreed, and they would all have died.

Mujāhid said: it is the saying of a person to his child, his property, when he is angry: "O Allah, destroy him! O Allah, do not bless him in it, and curse him!" A man may make such a prayer against himself, his child, his family or his property, with what he would dislike to be answered.

﴿Inna fī ikhtilāf al-layl wa-al-nahār wa-mā khalaqa Allāh fī al-samāwāt wa-al-arḍ la-āyātin li-qawmin yattaqūn﴾: Indeed in the alternation of night and day, and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, there are signs for a people who fear Allah, meaning who are certain, and so know and affirm.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the people of Mecca said, "Bring us a sign so that we may believe in you." So Allah revealed this verse.

﴿Inna alladhīna lā yarjūna liqāʾanā﴾: Indeed those who do not hope for meeting Us, meaning they do not fear Our punishment and do not hope for Our reward. Rajāʾ can mean dread and fear. ﴿Wa-raḍū bi-al-ḥayāt al-dunyā﴾: and are content with the life of this world, choosing it as their abode. ﴿Wa-iṭma'annū bihā﴾: and feel at rest in it, settling into it.

Qatada said concerning this verse: if you wish, you will see a man of this world who rejoices for it, grieves for it, is pleased for it and is angry for it.

Mujāhid and Muqātil said: ﴿yahdīhim﴾ means He will guide them with light on the path (ṣirāṭ) to Paradise; He will make for them a light by which they walk.

He says: 'I am your deed.' So it becomes for him a light and a guide to Paradise. When the disbeliever comes out of his grave, his deed takes for him an evil form and a foul smell. The meaning is: they were excessive in their worship and excessive in their expenditure.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed this world is green and sweet, and Allah has made you its successors in it, so He will look at how you act."

Qatada: it has been related to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Allah has spoken the truth; our Lord did not make us successors except that He might look at our deeds. So show Allah good deeds, by night and by day, in secret and in public."

Thābit al-Bunānī narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Layla that ʿAwf ibn Mālik said to Abu Bakr: "I saw in a dream, as one who sleeps sees, that something was lowered to me from the sky, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took hold of it, and then it was returned, and Abu Bakr took hold of it; then people measured around the pulpit, and ʿUmar was found to be three cubits more than the pulpit." ʿUmar said: "Leave us from your dream; we have no need of it." When ʿUmar became caliph, he said: "Tell me your dream, O ʿAwf." He said: "Do you have any need of my dream?" He said: "Did you not forbid me?" He said: "Woe to you! I disliked that you should announce to the caliph of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) his own death." Then he related the dream to him, until when he reached the measuring of the people around the pulpit with these three cubits, ʿUmar said: "As for the first, you will indeed be caliph. As for the second, he will not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of Allah. As for the third, he will be a martyr." Then he said: "Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then We made you successors in the earth after them﴾ up to His saying ﴿so that He may see how you act﴾. So you have been made a successor, O son of Umm ʿUmar; so look how you act." As for his saying: "I will not fear in Allah the blame of any blamer," this is as Allah wills; and as for his saying: "I will be a martyr," by the life of ʿUmar it is martyrdom, while the Muslims surround him. Then he said: "Indeed Allah is powerful over whatever He wills."

He it is who made the sun a radiance by day and the moon a light by night. Al-Kalbi said: their faces shine upon the people of the seven heavens, and their backs upon the people of the seven earths.

[Most readers recited ﴿ḍiyā'an﴾ with a single hamza.] It is narrated from Ibn Kathir: ﴿ḍi'ā'an﴾ with a hamza on the ya', but there is no basis for it, because its ya' was originally a fatha-vowelled waw, the middle radical of the verb. It was said: qaddara is of the type that takes two objects, yet it did not say qaddarahumā. The sun and the moon have been mentioned, and there are two possibilities. The first is that the pronoun refers to the moon alone, through the crescents by which the passing of months and years is known, not the sun. The second is that one of the two has been mentioned and the other omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [9:62]. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith when he said: ﴿Allāhumma in kāna hādhā huwa al-ḥaqq min ʿindika fa-amṭir ʿalaynā ḥijāratan min al-samāʾ﴾: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky" [8:32]. The meaning is: they were excessive in their worship and excessive in their expenditure.

Shahr ibn Ḥawshab: I read in some books that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to the two angels charged with recording: "Do not write anything against My servant in a state of his distress."

The common readers recited ﴿la-quḍiya ilayhim ājāluhum﴾ with a ḍamma on the qāf and the lām, as a passive verb with a nominative subject. ʿAwf, ʿĪsā, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb recited it with a fatḥa on the qāf and the lām. al-Aʿmash recited: ﴿la-quḍīnā﴾, and so it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah.

It was said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith when he said: ﴿Allāhumma in kāna hādhā huwa al-ḥaqq min ʿindika fa-amṭir ʿalaynā ḥijāratan min al-samāʾ﴾: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky" [8:32]. This is supported by His saying: ﴿fa-nadharu alladhīna lā yarjūna liqāʾanā﴾: so We leave those who do not hope for meeting Us, who do not fear resurrection and reckoning and do not hope for reward, ﴿fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn﴾: wandering blindly in their rebellion.

﴿Wa-idhā massa al-insān al-ḍurr﴾: and when harm touches man, meaning hardship and distress, ﴿daʿānā li-janbihi﴾: he calls upon Us, lying on his side, ﴿aw qāʿidan aw qāʾiman﴾: or sitting or standing. He means all his states, because a person does not go beyond one of these conditions. ﴿Falammā kashafnā ʿanhu ḍurrahu﴾: but when We remove and relieve him of his harm, ﴿marra kaʾan lam yadʿunā ilā ḍurrin massah﴾: he goes on as though he had never called upon Us to remove a harm that had touched him, meaning he continues in his former way. It was said: when harm touches him, he forgets what he was in of hardship and affliction, and abandons thanks and supplication. al-Akhfash said: ﴿ka-an lam yadʿunā﴾ and ﴿ka-an lam yalbathū﴾ and similar, where ka-anna is the heavy form and the emphatic: "as if he had not called upon Us." ﴿Kadhālika zuyyina lil-musrifīn﴾: thus it was made attractive to the wasteful, meaning: just as the call in time of affliction was made attractive to this man, and turning away in time of ease, so too the wasteful were made to see as fine their striving in disbelief and disobedience. ﴿Mā kānū yaʿmalūn﴾: what they did of disbelief and disobedience. Wastefulness (isrāf) may be of the self. In one reading: he wasted himself, making it a worshipper of an idol, and wasted his property by making it [unprofitable, without good]. The meaning is: they were excessive in their worship and excessive in their expenditure.

﴿Wa-laqad ahlaknā al-qurūn min qablikum﴾: We destroyed generations before you, meaning the past nations. Ibn ʿAbbas said: between the two horns [generations] were twenty-eight years. ﴿Lammā ẓalamū﴾: when they did wrong, that is, they associated partners with Allah. ﴿Wa-jāʾathum rusuluhum bi-al-bayyināt﴾: their messengers came to them with clear proofs, ﴿wa-mā kānū li-yuʾminū﴾: but they would not believe. ﴿Kadhālika﴾: thus, as We destroyed them for their disbelief and their denial of their messengers, ﴿najzī﴾: We destroy ﴿al-qawm al-mujrimīn﴾: the wicked people, the polytheists, whose denial of Muḥammad (ﷺ) warns the disbelievers of Mecca of the punishment of the earlier, denying nations.

﴿Thumma jaʿalnākum khalāʾifa fī al-arḍ min baʿdihim﴾: then We made you successors in the earth after them, meaning after the generations We destroyed, ﴿li-nanẓura﴾: so that We may see, that is, so that We may know, ﴿kayfa taʿmalūn﴾: how you act, though He knows them best.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed this world is green and sweet, and Allah has made you its successors in it, so He will look at how you act."

Qatada: it has been related to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Allah has spoken the truth; our Lord did not make us successors except that He might look at our deeds. So show Allah good deeds, by night and by day, in secret and in public."

Thābit al-Bunānī narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Layla that ʿAwf ibn Mālik said to Abu Bakr: "I saw in a dream, as one who sleeps sees, that something was lowered to me from the sky, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took hold of it, and then it was returned, and Abu Bakr took hold of it; then people measured around the pulpit, and ʿUmar was found to be three cubits more than the pulpit." ʿUmar said: "Leave us from your dream; we have no need of it." When ʿUmar became caliph, he said: "Tell me your dream, O ʿAwf." He said: "Do you have any need of my dream?" He said: "Did you not forbid me?" He said: "Woe to you! I disliked that you should announce to the caliph of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) his own death." Then he related the dream to him, until when he reached the measuring of the people around the pulpit with these three cubits, ʿUmar said: "As for the first, you will indeed be caliph. As for the second, he will not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of Allah. As for the third, he will be a martyr." Then he said: "Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then We made you successors in the earth after them﴾ up to His saying ﴿so that He may see how you act﴾. So you have been made a successor, O son of Umm ʿUmar; so look how you act." As for his saying: "I will not fear in Allah the blame of any blamer," this is as Allah wills; and as for his saying: "I will be a martyr," by the life of ʿUmar it is martyrdom, while the Muslims surround him. Then he said: "Indeed Allah is powerful over whatever He wills."

Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 15–20:

﴿When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say...﴾ Qatada said: this refers to the polytheists of Makkah. Muqatil said:

They were five men: Abd Allah ibn Umayya al-Makhzumi, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Mukarriz ibn Hafs, Amr ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Qays al-Amiri, and al-As ibn Amir ibn Hashim. They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Bring a Qur'an in which there is no abandoning the worship of al-Lat, al-Uzza, Manat and Hubal, and in which there is nothing against them," that is, "change it," meaning "say it from your own accord."

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the mockers. They said: "O Muhammad, bring a Qur'an other than this, in which there is nothing that angers us, or change it: put a verse of mercy in place of a verse of punishment, or a verse of punishment in place of a verse of mercy, or make the forbidden lawful and the lawful forbidden."

﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I only follow what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.﴾ "On my own accord" means from my own self and from my own side. "I only follow what is revealed to me" means I obey Him in what I command you and forbid you.

﴿Say: If God had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you know it.﴾ "Make you know it" means inform you of it. Al-Hasan recited: "wa-la adraatukum" [[There is a dispute concerning the attribution to al-Hasan: whether it is "adra'atkum" with a hamza or without, "adraatukum." It has a detailed treatment; see the tafsir of al-Qurtubi: 8/321.]]. This is the dialect of the Banu Uqayl, who convert the yā' into an alif, saying "a'taat" for "a'tayt" (I gave), "labbaat" for "labbayt" (I answered the call), "jaaraah" and "naasaah" for "jaariyah" (slave-girl) and "naasiyah" (forelock). Al-Mufaddal recited:

"They have indeed informed the people of Yamama, Tayy, of a war like the forelock of the bright-white, distinguished horse."

Zayd al-Khayl said:

"By your life, I do not fear poverty so long as there remains on the earth a man of Qays who drives camels."

That is, "so long as there remains." Another said:

"I rebuked him, and we said: we will not frighten a rebuker. Indeed, the one who is misguided, when he is forbidden, does not heed."

That is, "when he is forbidden" [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/127.]].

Al-Bazzi narrated from Ibn Kathir: "wa-la adraakum," with the short vowel, as an affirmation, meaning: "nor would you have known it by my work without my reciting it to you." [[This is the lam of emphasis, entering upon the alif of af'ala.]] Ibn Abbas recited "wa-la adraatukum," with the yā' converted to alif, from the root of warning (al-inḏār), and this is also the reading of al-Hasan.

﴿Indeed I have remained among you a lifetime,﴾ that is, a span of forty years, ﴿before it.﴾ That is, before the revelation of the Qur'an, and I did not bring you anything. ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ That it is not from me.

Ibn Abbas said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was given prophethood at forty years of age; he remained in Makkah thirteen years and in Madinah ten years, and he died at sixty-three years of age.

﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, claiming that He has a partner, or a consort, or a son, or denies His signs﴾ (Muhammad and the Qur'an)? ﴿Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.﴾ The polytheists will neither be safe nor be saved.

﴿And they worship, besides God, that which neither harms them﴾ if they disobey Him, ﴿nor benefits them﴾ if they obey Him. This refers to the idols. ﴿And they say: These are our intercessors with God.﴾

﴿Say: Do you inform God of what He does not know in the heavens or in the earth?﴾ Most readers recite "tunabbi'ūna" with the doubled consonant (tashdid). Abu al-Shamal al-Adawi recited "tunbi'ūna" without it, and both are two dialects: nabaa yanbi'u, and anba'anī inbā' carry the same meaning, and their active participle is the same.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿They said: Who informed you of this? He said: The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me﴾ [[Surah al-Tahrim: 3.]] ﴿of what He does not know﴾, meaning of what God, exalted is He, does not know to be sound and real, and which does not exist ﴿in the heavens or in the earth.﴾ The meaning of the verse is: Do you inform God that He has a partner, or that He has an intercessor in His presence without His permission? God does not know that He has a partner in the heavens or in the earth, because He has no partner, and so He does not know it. A parallel is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ [[Surah al-Ra'd: 33.]]

Then He declared Himself free of imperfection, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ Yahya ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, Abu Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited "tushrikūna" with the tā' here and in surahs al-Nahl and al-Rum. This is the choice of Abu Ubayd, because of the address that precedes it. The rest recited all of them with the yā', and Abu Hatim chose it, saying: "Thus were we taught it."

﴿And mankind was not but one community﴾ upon one religion, Islam, the religion of Adam (peace be upon him), until one of the two sons of Adam killed his brother. ﴿Then they differed.﴾ This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

Ibn Abbas said: between Adam and Noah were ten centuries, all upon a law of truth. ﴿Then they differed in the time of Noah,﴾ so God sent Noah to them. It was also said: they were one community gathered upon monotheism on the Day of the Covenant.

It was also said: they were the people of Noah's ark [[The one who said this was al-Waqidi.]]. Abu Raq said: they were one community upon the religion of Islam in the time of Noah (peace be upon him) after the flood. Ata' said: they were upon one religion, Islam, from the time of Abraham (peace be upon him) until Amr ibn Yahya changed it [[He was the first to change the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him) and to worship idols among the Arabs.]]. Ata' also said: the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) confirms the soundness of these interpretations: ﴿And mankind was not but one community upon guidance, then they differed concerning it.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: ﴿And mankind was not but one community﴾, disbelieving, in the time of Abraham, ﴿then they differed﴾, that is, they separated: believer and disbeliever.

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, namely that He appointed for this world a term for every community, a fixed time it cannot exceed. Abu Raq said this, and al-Kalbi said: it is that God postponed this community and does not destroy them with punishment in this world. It was also said: it is that He does not seize them until the proof has been established.

Al-Hasan said: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾ that passed in His decree, that He would not judge among them concerning what they differed about, by reward and punishment, except on the Resurrection.

﴿The matter would have been decided between them﴾ in this world: He would have admitted the believers to Paradise by their deeds and the disbelievers into the Fire by their disbelief. But a term from God had preceded, so He made their appointment the Day of Resurrection.

Abu Raq said: ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ means He would have established the Hour upon them. It was also said: the matter would have been the fear of their destruction. Isa ibn Umar recited "laqaḍiya baynahum" with a fatḥah, because of the phrase ﴿from your Lord﴾ [[The text reads: "min rabbika... fīmā fīhi yakhtalifūn."]], concerning what they differ about.

﴿And they say﴾, meaning the people of Makkah: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ That is, upon Muhammad. ﴿So say, O Muhammad, to them:﴾ You asked me for the unseen, ﴿the unseen belongs only to God.﴾ None of you knows what will be done except Him. It was also said: "the unseen" is the descent of the sign: when it will descend, it descends. ﴿So wait﴾ for the descent of the sign, ﴿indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ for its descent. It was also said: ﴿So wait﴾ for God's judgment between us by manifesting the truth over falsehood. Al-Hasan said: ﴿So wait﴾ for the promises of Satan, for they were upon an appointment with Iblis, concerning what he promises them and what he gives them hope of. ﴿Indeed I am with you among those who wait.﴾ So God fulfilled His promise and gave victory to His servant.

﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, claiming that He has a partner, or a consort, or a son, or denies His signs﴾ (Muhammad and the Qur'an)? ﴿Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.﴾ The polytheists will neither be safe nor be saved.

﴿And they worship, besides God, that which neither harms them﴾ if they disobey Him, ﴿nor benefits them﴾ if they obey Him. This refers to the idols. ﴿And they say: These are our intercessors with God.﴾

﴿Say: Do you inform God of what He does not know in the heavens or in the earth?﴾ Most readers recite "tunabbi'ūna" with the doubled consonant (tashdid). Abu al-Shamal al-Adawi recited "tunbi'ūna" without it, and both are two dialects: nabaa yanbi'u, and anba'anī inbā' carry the same meaning, and their active participle is the same.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿They said: Who informed you of this? He said: The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me﴾ [[Surah al-Tahrim: 3.]] ﴿of what He does not know﴾, meaning of what God, exalted is He, does not know to be sound and real, and which does not exist ﴿in the heavens or in the earth.﴾ The meaning of the verse is: Do you inform God that He has a partner, or that He has an intercessor in His presence without His permission? God does not know that He has a partner in the heavens or in the earth, because He has no partner, and so He does not know it. A parallel is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ [[Surah al-Ra'd: 33.]]

Then He declared Himself free of imperfection, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ Yahya ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, Abu Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited "tushrikūna" with the tā' here and in surahs al-Nahl and al-Rum. This is the choice of Abu Ubayd, because of the address that precedes it. The rest recited all of them with the yā', and Abu Hatim chose it, saying: "Thus were we taught it."

﴿And mankind was not but one community﴾ upon one religion, Islam, the religion of Adam (peace be upon him), until one of the two sons of Adam killed his brother. ﴿Then they differed.﴾ This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

Ibn Abbas said: between Adam and Noah were ten centuries, all upon a law of truth. ﴿Then they differed in the time of Noah,﴾ so God sent Noah to them. It was also said: they were one community gathered upon monotheism on the Day of the Covenant.

It was also said: they were the people of Noah's ark [[The one who said this was al-Waqidi.]]. Abu Raq said: they were one community upon the religion of Islam in the time of Noah (peace be upon him) after the flood. Ata' said: they were upon one religion, Islam, from the time of Abraham (peace be upon him) until Amr ibn Yahya changed it [[He was the first to change the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him) and to worship idols among the Arabs.]]. Ata' also said: the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) confirms the soundness of these interpretations: ﴿And mankind was not but one community upon guidance, then they differed concerning it.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: ﴿And mankind was not but one community﴾, disbelieving, in the time of Abraham, ﴿then they differed﴾, that is, they separated: believer and disbeliever.

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, namely that He appointed for this world a term for every community, a fixed time it cannot exceed. Abu Raq said this, and al-Kalbi said: it is that God postponed this community and does not destroy them with punishment in this world. It was also said: it is that He does not seize them until the proof has been established.

Al-Hasan said: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾ that passed in His decree, that He would not judge among them concerning what they differed about, by reward and punishment, except on the Resurrection.

﴿The matter would have been decided between them﴾ in this world: He would have admitted the believers to Paradise by their deeds and the disbelievers into the Fire by their disbelief. But a term from God had preceded, so He made their appointment the Day of Resurrection.

Abu Raq said: ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ means He would have established the Hour upon them. It was also said: the matter would have been the fear of their destruction. Isa ibn Umar recited "laqaḍiya baynahum" with a fatḥah, because of the phrase ﴿from your Lord﴾ [[The text reads: "min rabbika... fīmā fīhi yakhtalifūn."]], concerning what they differ about.

﴿And they say﴾, meaning the people of Makkah: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ That is, upon Muhammad. ﴿So say, O Muhammad, to them:﴾ You asked me for the unseen, ﴿the unseen belongs only to God.﴾ None of you knows what will be done except Him. It was also said: "the unseen" is the descent of the sign: when it will descend, it descends. ﴿So wait﴾ for the descent of the sign, ﴿indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ for its descent. It was also said: ﴿So wait﴾ for God's judgment between us by manifesting the truth over falsehood. Al-Hasan said: ﴿So wait﴾ for the promises of Satan, for they were upon an appointment with Iblis, concerning what he promises them and what he gives them hope of. ﴿Indeed I am with you among those who wait.﴾ So God fulfilled His promise and gave victory to His servant.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (*al-Jawahir al-Hisan*) on Surah 10, verses 21–25:

﴿And when We let people taste mercy after adversity has touched them,﴾ meaning the disbelievers. Mercy here means ease and prosperity after hardship and affliction. It was also said that it refers to rain after drought. ﴿Behold, they scheme against Our signs.﴾ Mujahid said: this means mockery and denial. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: they do not say, "This is the provision of Allah." Rather, they say, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising (nawʾ)," which is attributing the blessings to other than Allah. This is His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it?﴾ [56:82]. ﴿Say: Allah is swifter in scheming﴾, meaning quicker in punishment, stronger in seizing, and more capable of requital. Muqatil said: "swifter in contrivance (ṣanīʿ)." ﴿Indeed, Our messengers (i.e., the guardian angels) record what you scheme.﴾ The majority of readers recite it with the letter ta' (tamkurūna, "you scheme"), in accordance with His words ﴿Say...﴾ (addressed in the second person). The recitation of al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and Yaʿqub reads it with the letter yaʾ (yamkurūna, "they scheme"), in accordance with His words ﴿Behold, they...﴾. This is also the transmission of Harun from Abu ʿAmr. [Harun al-ʿAtaki transmitted from Abu ʿAmr the reading yamkurūna with yaʾ.]

﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea.﴾ That is, He carries you through the sea and makes you able to travel. Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿yunshirukum﴾ with nūn, from "nashr" (spreading out, dispersing), meaning [spreading] you on land, on the backs of animals, and on sea, on ships. ﴿Until, when you are in ships﴾, meaning in the boats, whether the word is singular or plural. ʿIsa read ﴿al-fulk﴾ with a ḍamma on the lam.

﴿And they sail with them﴾, meaning the ships sail with the people. This is a direct address (khiṭāb) of description that shifts from address to narration. ﴿with a pleasant wind, and they rejoice in it.﴾ That is, the wind came upon the ship (al-falak). This is the answer to His saying "until, when there comes upon them a violent wind." It is said: "ʿaṣafat al-rīḥ" and "aʿṣafat," and rīḥ (wind) is both masculine and feminine. It was said: He did not say ʿāṣifa (feminine form), because the wind is specifically associated with violent blowing. It was also said: it is in the relative form, meaning "possessing violence." ﴿And the waves come upon them from every place﴾, meaning the people on board the ship. The "mawj" is the movement of water and its mixtures. ﴿And they think that they are encompassed﴾, meaning they became certain (wa-ẓannū wa-aydaqū) that they were surrounded by destruction. ﴿They call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾, meaning in supplication, not to their idols. Their refuge was to Allah alone, not to them.

Al-Thawri narrated from al-Aʿmash, from ʿAmr ibn Murrah, from Abu ʿUbayd, regarding His words ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾: they used to say in their supplication, "Ahyā shirāhyā," and its explanation is "O Living, O Self-Subsisting" [see Taj al-ʿArus 9/394, where its vocalization is disputed].

﴿If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful.﴾ That is, O our Lord, rescue us (khalliṣnā) from this violent wind; we will surely be among those who give thanks to You through faith and obedience. ﴿But when He delivered them, behold, they commit injustice in the earth without right.﴾ They oppress and transgress to what is other than the command of Allah. ﴿O mankind, your injustice is only against yourselves.﴾ Its harm returns to them now, and its consequence will surely reach them. The speech ends here, as in His saying: ﴿They did not remain but an hour of a day. [This is a notification.]﴾ [46:35]. That is, this is a notification (balāgh). It was also said that it is continuous speech: "al-baghy" is the subject (mubtada'), and "matāʿ" is its predicate. His words ﴿against yourselves﴾ are a complement of "matāʿ," and the meaning is: "Your injustice against yourselves is the enjoyment of the life of this world," and it is not suitable as provision for the Hereafter, because you have deserved the anger of Allah.

Ibn Ishaq and Hafs read ﴿matāʿan﴾ with fatḥa, as a state (ḥāl). ﴿Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

﴿Indeed, the example of the life of this world﴾, in its passing and cessation, ﴿is like water which We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mixed with it, of which men and animals eat﴾, from grains, herbs and fruits, and livestock from grass and pasture.

﴿Until, when the earth takes on its adornment﴾, its beauty and splendor, ﴿and is decorated﴾. This is the reading of the majority. What confirms it is the reading of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud: "wa-tazayyanat." Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi and al-Dahhak read "wa-izzānat" on the pattern of "ijjāzat." ʿAwf ibn Abi Jamilah said: "Our shaykhs used to recite it that way" [see Tafsir al-Qurtubi 8/327]. "Izyānat" is like "isswaddat." Abu Raja', Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Shaʿbi, al-Hasan and al-Aʿraj read "wa-uzyinat" on the pattern of "uf'alat," with the alif cut [with lightening]. Qutrub said: its meaning is "it brought the adornment upon it," like their saying "aḥabba fa-udhimma" and "udhkirat al-mar'ah fa-unthat."

﴿And its people think that they are able to harvest it.﴾ He reports about the earth, meaning the plants, since they are understood. It was also said: it refers to the produce; and it was said: to the adornment. ﴿There comes to it Our command﴾, meaning Our decree for its destruction, ﴿by night or by day, and We make it a harvested field, as if it had not flourished yesterday.﴾ Its origin is from "ghanī al-makān" when one stays in a place and inhabits it. Muqatil said: "taghumm" (it does not exist). The majority read "taghna" with the letter tāʾ, due to the feminine form of "the earth." Qatadah read it with yaʾ, taking the reference to "the adornment" [in al-Zad al-Masir: meaning the harvest].

﴿Thus We detail the signs for a people who give thought.﴾

﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾. Qatadah said: "al-Salam" is Allah, and His abode is Paradise. It was also said: "al-salam" and "al-salama" are the same, like "al-lidhādh" and "al-ladhdhah," and "al-riḍāʿ" and "al-riḍāʿah." The poet said:

"Greetings of safety to Umm Bakr... and is there for you, after your kin, any peace?" [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 8/328, where it reads "qawmik" instead of "rahtik"].

Paradise is called the Abode of Peace because whoever enters it is safe from afflictions. Allah said: ﴿Enter it in peace, secure﴾ [15:46]. Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: it is so called because whoever enters it is safe from severance and separation. It was also said: it means greeting; one says "salama taslīman and salāman," just as one says "kallama takliman and kalāman." Paradise is called the Abode of Peace because its people greet one another, and the angels greet them. Al-Hasan said: the greeting does not cease for the people of Paradise, and it is their salutation.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it is so called because whoever enters it is greeted by the Master, because Allah knows what the people of Paradise have of remembrance of sins and awe before the Knower of the Unseen. So He begins with them with greeting and salutation, bringing them near, showing familiarity and welcome.

Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us one day and said: "I saw in a dream as if Jibril was at my head and Mikail at my feet. One of them said to the other: 'Give him a parable.' He said: 'Listen, may your ear hear; understand, may the understanding of your heart understand. Your parable and the parable of your community is like the parable of a king who built a house, then constructed a room in it, then prepared a feast in it, then sent a messenger calling them to his food. Some of them answered the messenger, and some of them left him. So Allah is the King, the house is Islam, the room is Paradise, and you, O Muhammad, are the messenger. Whoever answers you enters Islam, whoever enters Islam enters Paradise, and whoever enters Paradise eats of what is in it.'" [78] [Sunan al-Tirmidhi 4/223].

Yahya ibn Muʿadh said: "O son of Adam, Allah has called you to the Abode of Peace, so look from where you will respond to Him. If you respond to Him from your worldly life, you will enter it; if you respond from your grave, you will be prevented from it."

Then He said: ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ He made the invitation general to show His proof, and made guidance specific, out of independence from His creation. It was also said: the invitation to the Abode is general, because it is the path to the blessing; and the guidance to the path is specific, because it is the path to the Benefactor.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. ﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَنَّةِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ما لَهُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عاصِمٍ﴾ ("Humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah"): i.e., from the punishment of Allah; *min* here is for emphasis. "Protector" means one who prevents.

﴿كَأَنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعاً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِماً﴾ ("As if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night"): most readers read *qit'an* with a fatha on the *ṭā'*, the plural of *qit'ah*. In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهُمْ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا مَكانَكُمْ أَنْتُمْ وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ ("And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all; then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners'"): i.e., stand and remain in your places and do not move. The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

﴿وَقالَ شُرَكاؤُهُمْ ما كُنْتُمْ إِيَّانا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("And their partners will say: 'You did not used to worship us.'"): they will say, "Yes, you did worship us." Then the idols will say:

﴿فَكَفى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيداً بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنْ كُنَّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكُمْ لَغافِلِينَ﴾ ("Sufficient is Allah as witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship"): i.e., we were not aware of your worship of us, except that we were heedless, did not hear, did not see, and did not understand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿هُنالِكَ تَبْلُوا كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾ ("There, every soul will experience what it had sent forward"): *tabluw* means "it will test/inform," and it was also said: "it will know." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾: its record. It was also said: the meaning is that it follows what it sent forward of good and evil. Ibn Zayd said: [it is] "cooperates." ﴿وَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلاهُمُ الْحَقِّ﴾ ("And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master"); ﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ ("And what they used to invent will vanish from them"): i.e., the deities will perish [from them].

﴿قُلْ مَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ ("Say: 'Who provides for you from the sky'"): the rain; ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: the plants. ﴿أَمَّنْ يَمْلِكُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصارَ﴾ ("Or who controls hearing and sight?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ وَيُخْرِجُ الْمَيِّتَ مِنَ الْحَيِّ﴾ ("And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ ("And who arranges the affair?"). ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("They will say: 'Allah'"): the One who did these things. ﴿فَقُلْ أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Say: 'Will you not then fear [Him]?'"): i.e., will you not fear His punishment for your polytheism?

﴿فَذلِكُمُ اللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ الْحَقُّ﴾ ("Then that is Allah, your true Lord"): the One who does these things. ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الْحَقِّ إِلَّا الضَّلالُ فَأَنَّى تُصْرَفُونَ﴾ ("So what is there after the truth but error? Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

﴿كَذلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("Thus the word of your Lord has been justified"): al-Kalbi explained it as "thus," the same in all of the Qur'an. *Haqqat* means "became due"; *kalimat Rabbika* means His decree and His prior knowledge.

Al-A'raj read *kalimāt* ("words"). ﴿عَلَى الَّذِينَ فَسَقُوا﴾ ("upon those who defied"): i.e., disbelieved. ﴿أَنَّهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("that they will not believe").

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, the assimilated *yā'* changed to *hā'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. 'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

Yahya ibn Adam narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a kasrah on the *hā'* and the *yā'*, and a shaddah on the *dāl*, [to follow] the kasrah with the kasrah. It was also said: it is according to the dialect of those who read *na'budu* and *nasta'īnu*, and *lan tamassanā al-nār*, and similar words.

Abu 'Amr read between fatha and *jazm*, according to his method of *ikhfā'* (partial articulation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يُهْدى﴾ ("unless he is guided"): the meaning of the verse has two aspects. One group directed it to the leaders and the misguided ones: meaning, they do not guide unless they are guided. Others understood it as referring to the idols, and said: the sense of the expression is that it does not move unless it is carried and transported from its place, unless it is moved, as in the words of the poet:

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

﴿فَما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ﴾ ("What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").
