Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾: its record. It was also said: the meaning is that it follows what it sent forward of good and evil. Ibn Zayd said: [it is] "cooperates." ﴿وَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلاهُمُ الْحَقِّ﴾ ("And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master"); ﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ ("And what they used to invent will vanish from them"): i.e., the deities will perish [from them].

﴿قُلْ مَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ ("Say: 'Who provides for you from the sky'"): the rain; ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: the plants. ﴿أَمَّنْ يَمْلِكُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصارَ﴾ ("Or who controls hearing and sight?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ وَيُخْرِجُ الْمَيِّتَ مِنَ الْحَيِّ﴾ ("And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ ("And who arranges the affair?"). ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("They will say: 'Allah'"): the One who did these things. ﴿فَقُلْ أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Say: 'Will you not then fear [Him]?'"): i.e., will you not fear His punishment for your polytheism?

﴿فَذلِكُمُ اللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ الْحَقُّ﴾ ("Then that is Allah, your true Lord"): the One who does these things. ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الْحَقِّ إِلَّا الضَّلالُ فَأَنَّى تُصْرَفُونَ﴾ ("So what is there after the truth but error? Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

﴿كَذلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("Thus the word of your Lord has been justified"): al-Kalbi explained it as "thus," the same in all of the Qur'an. *Haqqat* means "became due"; *kalimat Rabbika* means His decree and His prior knowledge.

Al-A'raj read *kalimāt* ("words"). ﴿عَلَى الَّذِينَ فَسَقُوا﴾ ("upon those who defied"): i.e., disbelieved. ﴿أَنَّهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("that they will not believe").

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, the assimilated *yā'* changed to *hā'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. 'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

Yahya ibn Adam narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a kasrah on the *hā'* and the *yā'*, and a shaddah on the *dāl*, [to follow] the kasrah with the kasrah. It was also said: it is according to the dialect of those who read *na'budu* and *nasta'īnu*, and *lan tamassanā al-nār*, and similar words.

Abu 'Amr read between fatha and *jazm*, according to his method of *ikhfā'* (partial articulation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يُهْدى﴾ ("unless he is guided"): the meaning of the verse has two aspects. One group directed it to the leaders and the misguided ones: meaning, they do not guide unless they are guided. Others understood it as referring to the idols, and said: the sense of the expression is that it does not move unless it is carried and transported from its place, unless it is moved, as in the words of the poet:

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

﴿فَما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ﴾ ("What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

'Ata' narrated from him concerning ﴿هي﴾ (the reward): one good deed is counted as one, and *al-ziyadah* is the multiplication by ten of its like, up to seven hundred times. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/141–142.]]

Juwaybir narrated from al-Layth, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: *al-husna* is the (divine) look, and *al-ziyadah* is the gazing. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Mujahid said: *al-husna* is one good deed like one good deed, and *al-ziyadah* is ﴿مَغْفِرَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوانٌ﴾ ("forgiveness from Allah and approval"). Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

Mansur ibn 'Ammar narrated from Yazid ibn Shajarah, who said: *al-ziyadah* is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every kind of rare thing, and says to them: "What do you wish that I should rain upon you?" And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. Qatadah said: it is grief and gloom. Ibn Abi Layla said: this is after their looking at their Lord.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَنَّةِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ما لَهُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عاصِمٍ﴾ ("Humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah"): i.e., from the punishment of Allah; *min* here is for emphasis. "Protector" means one who prevents.

﴿كَأَنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعاً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِماً﴾ ("As if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night"): most readers read *qit'an* with a fatha on the *ṭā'*, the plural of *qit'ah*. In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. **Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

'Ata' narrated from him concerning ﴿هي﴾ (the reward): one good deed is counted as one, and *al-ziyadah* is the multiplication by ten of its like, up to seven hundred times. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/141–142.]]

Juwaybir narrated from al-Layth, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: *al-husna* is the (divine) look, and *al-ziyadah* is the gazing. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Mujahid said: *al-husna* is one good deed like one good deed, and *al-ziyadah* is ﴿مَغْفِرَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوانٌ﴾ ("forgiveness from Allah and approval"). Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

Mansur ibn 'Ammar narrated from Yazid ibn Shajarah, who said: *al-ziyadah* is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every kind of rare thing, and says to them: "What do you wish that I should rain upon you?" And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. Qatadah said: it is grief and gloom. Ibn Abi Layla said: this is after their looking at their Lord.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَنَّةِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ما لَهُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عاصِمٍ﴾ ("Humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah"): i.e., from the punishment of Allah; *min* here is for emphasis. "Protector" means one who prevents.

﴿كَأَنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعاً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِماً﴾ ("As if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night"): most readers read *qit'an* with a fatha on the *ṭā'*, the plural of *qit'ah*. In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهُمْ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا مَكانَكُمْ أَنْتُمْ وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ ("And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all; then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners'"): i.e., stand and remain in your places and do not move. The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

﴿وَقالَ شُرَكاؤُهُمْ ما كُنْتُمْ إِيَّانا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("And their partners will say: 'You did not used to worship us.'"): they will say, "Yes, you did worship us." Then the idols will say:

﴿فَكَفى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيداً بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنْ كُنَّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكُمْ لَغافِلِينَ﴾ ("Sufficient is Allah as witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship"): i.e., we were not aware of your worship of us, except that we were heedless, did not hear, did not see, and did not understand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿هُنالِكَ تَبْلُوا كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾ ("There, every soul will experience what it had sent forward"): *tabluw* means "it will test/inform," and it was also said: "it will know." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾: its record. It was also said: the meaning is that it follows what it sent forward of good and evil. Ibn Zayd said: [it is] "cooperates." ﴿وَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلاهُمُ الْحَقِّ﴾ ("And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master"); ﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ ("And what they used to invent will vanish from them"): i.e., the deities will perish [from them].

﴿قُلْ مَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ ("Say: 'Who provides for you from the sky'"): the rain; ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: the plants. ﴿أَمَّنْ يَمْلِكُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصارَ﴾ ("Or who controls hearing and sight?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ وَيُخْرِجُ الْمَيِّتَ مِنَ الْحَيِّ﴾ ("And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ ("And who arranges the affair?"). ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("They will say: 'Allah'"): the One who did these things. ﴿فَقُلْ أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Say: 'Will you not then fear [Him]?'"): i.e., will you not fear His punishment for your polytheism?

﴿فَذلِكُمُ اللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ الْحَقُّ﴾ ("Then that is Allah, your true Lord"): the One who does these things. ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الْحَقِّ إِلَّا الضَّلالُ فَأَنَّى تُصْرَفُونَ﴾ ("So what is there after the truth but error? Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

﴿كَذلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("Thus the word of your Lord has been justified"): al-Kalbi explained it as "thus," the same in all of the Qur'an. *Haqqat* means "became due"; *kalimat Rabbika* means His decree and His prior knowledge.

Al-A'raj read *kalimāt* ("words"). ﴿عَلَى الَّذِينَ فَسَقُوا﴾ ("upon those who defied"): i.e., disbelieved. ﴿أَنَّهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("that they will not believe").

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

He means: wherever it is carried.

How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. ﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ما لَهُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عاصِمٍ﴾ ("Humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah"): i.e., from the punishment of Allah; *min* here is for emphasis. "Protector" means one who prevents.

﴿كَأَنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعاً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِماً﴾ ("As if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night"): most readers read *qit'an* with a fatha on the *ṭā'*, the plural of *qit'ah*. In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهُمْ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا مَكانَكُمْ أَنْتُمْ وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ ("And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all; then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners'"): i.e., stand and remain in your places and do not move. The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

﴿وَقالَ شُرَكاؤُهُمْ ما كُنْتُمْ إِيَّانا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("And their partners will say: 'You did not used to worship us.'"): they will say, "Yes, you did worship us." Then the idols will say:

﴿فَكَفى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيداً بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنْ كُنَّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكُمْ لَغافِلِينَ﴾ ("Sufficient is Allah as witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship"): i.e., we were not aware of your worship of us, except that we were heedless, did not hear, did not see, and did not understand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿هُنالِكَ تَبْلُوا كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾ ("There, every soul will experience what it had sent forward"): *tabluw* means "it will test/inform," and it was also said: "it will know." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾: its record. It was also said: the meaning is that it follows what it sent forward of good and evil. Ibn Zayd said: [it is] "cooperates." ﴿وَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلاهُمُ الْحَقِّ﴾ ("And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master"); ﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ ("And what they used to invent will vanish from them"): i.e., the deities will perish [from them].

﴿قُلْ مَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ ("Say: 'Who provides for you from the sky'"): the rain; ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: the plants. ﴿أَمَّنْ يَمْلِكُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصارَ﴾ ("Or who controls hearing and sight?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ وَيُخْرِجُ الْمَيِّتَ مِنَ الْحَيِّ﴾ ("And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ ("And who arranges the affair?"). ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("They will say: 'Allah'"): the One who did these things. ﴿فَقُلْ أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Say: 'Will you not then fear [Him]?'"): i.e., will you not fear His punishment for your polytheism?

﴿فَذلِكُمُ اللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ الْحَقُّ﴾ ("Then that is Allah, your true Lord"): the One who does these things. ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الْحَقِّ إِلَّا الضَّلالُ فَأَنَّى تُصْرَفُونَ﴾ ("So what is there after the truth but error? Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

﴿كَذلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("Thus the word of your Lord has been justified"): al-Kalbi explained it as "thus," the same in all of the Qur'an. *Haqqat* means "became due"; *kalimat Rabbika* means His decree and His prior knowledge.

Al-A'raj read *kalimāt* ("words"). ﴿عَلَى الَّذِينَ فَسَقُوا﴾ ("upon those who defied"): i.e., disbelieved. ﴿أَنَّهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("that they will not believe").

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, the assimilated *yā'* changed to *hā'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. 'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

Yahya ibn Adam narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a kasrah on the *hā'* and the *yā'*, and a shaddah on the *dāl*, [to follow] the kasrah with the kasrah. It was also said: it is according to the dialect of those who read *na'budu* and *nasta'īnu*, and *lan tamassanā al-nār*, and similar words.

Abu 'Amr read between fatha and *jazm*, according to his method of *ikhfā'* (partial articulation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يُهْدى﴾ ("unless he is guided"): the meaning of the verse has two aspects. One group directed it to the leaders and the misguided ones: meaning, they do not guide unless they are guided. Others understood it as referring to the idols, and said: the sense of the expression is that it does not move unless it is carried and transported from its place, unless it is moved, as in the words of the poet:

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

﴿فَما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ﴾ ("What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

'Ata' narrated from him concerning ﴿هي﴾ (the reward): one good deed is counted as one, and *al-ziyadah* is the multiplication by ten of its like, up to seven hundred times. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/141–142.]]

Juwaybir narrated from al-Layth, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: *al-husna* is the (divine) look, and *al-ziyadah* is the gazing. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Mujahid said: *al-husna* is one good deed like one good deed, and *al-ziyadah* is ﴿مَغْفِرَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوانٌ﴾ ("forgiveness from Allah and approval"). Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

Mansur ibn 'Ammar narrated from Yazid ibn Shajarah, who said: *al-ziyadah* is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every kind of rare thing, and says to them: "What do you wish that I should rain upon you?" And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

﴿كَذلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("Thus the word of your Lord has been justified"): al-Kalbi explained it as "thus," the same in all of the Qur'an. *Haqqat* means "became due"; *kalimat Rabbika* means His decree and His prior knowledge.

Al-A'raj read *kalimāt* ("words"). ﴿عَلَى الَّذِينَ فَسَقُوا﴾ ("upon those who defied"): i.e., disbelieved. ﴿أَنَّهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("that they will not believe").

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, the assimilated *yā'* changed to *hā'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. 'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

Yahya ibn Adam narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a kasrah on the *hā'* and the *yā'*, and a shaddah on the *dāl*, [to follow] the kasrah with the kasrah. It was also said: it is according to the dialect of those who read *na'budu* and *nasta'īnu*, and *lan tamassanā al-nār*, and similar words.

Abu 'Amr read between fatha and *jazm*, according to his method of *ikhfā'* (partial articulation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يُهْدى﴾ ("unless he is guided"): the meaning of the verse has two aspects. One group directed it to the leaders and the misguided ones: meaning, they do not guide unless they are guided. Others understood it as referring to the idols, and said: the sense of the expression is that it does not move unless it is carried and transported from its place, unless it is moved, as in the words of the poet:

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

﴿فَما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ﴾ ("What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

'Ata' narrated from him concerning ﴿هي﴾ (the reward): one good deed is counted as one, and *al-ziyadah* is the multiplication by ten of its like, up to seven hundred times. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/141–142.]]

Juwaybir narrated from al-Layth, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: *al-husna* is the (divine) look, and *al-ziyadah* is the gazing. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Mujahid said: *al-husna* is one good deed like one good deed, and *al-ziyadah* is ﴿مَغْفِرَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوانٌ﴾ ("forgiveness from Allah and approval"). Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

Mansur ibn 'Ammar narrated from Yazid ibn Shajarah, who said: *al-ziyadah* is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every kind of rare thing, and says to them: "What do you wish that I should rain upon you?" And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. Qatadah said: it is grief and gloom. Ibn Abi Layla said: this is after their looking at their Lord.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَنَّةِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ما لَهُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عاصِمٍ﴾ ("Humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah"): i.e., from the punishment of Allah; *min* here is for emphasis. "Protector" means one who prevents.

﴿كَأَنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعاً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِماً﴾ ("As if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night"): most readers read *qit'an* with a fatha on the *ṭā'*, the plural of *qit'ah*. In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهُمْ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا مَكانَكُمْ أَنْتُمْ وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ ("And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all; then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners'"): i.e., stand and remain in your places and do not move. The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

﴿فَكَفى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيداً بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنْ كُنَّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكُمْ لَغافِلِينَ﴾ ("Sufficient is Allah as witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship"): i.e., we were not aware of your worship of us, except that we were heedless, did not hear, did not see, and did not understand.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

'Ata' narrated from him concerning ﴿هي﴾ (the reward): one good deed is counted as one, and *al-ziyadah* is the multiplication by ten of its like, up to seven hundred times. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/141–142.]]

Juwaybir narrated from al-Layth, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: *al-husna* is the (divine) look, and *al-ziyadah* is the gazing. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Mujahid said: *al-husna* is one good deed like one good deed, and *al-ziyadah* is ﴿مَغْفِرَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوانٌ﴾ ("forgiveness from Allah and approval"). Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

Mansur ibn 'Ammar narrated from Yazid ibn Shajarah, who said: *al-ziyadah* is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every kind of rare thing, and says to them: "What do you wish that I should rain upon you?" And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. Qatadah said: it is grief and gloom. Ibn Abi Layla said: this is after their looking at their Lord.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَنَّةِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ما لَهُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عاصِمٍ﴾ ("Humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah"): i.e., from the punishment of Allah; *min* here is for emphasis. "Protector" means one who prevents.

﴿كَأَنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعاً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِماً﴾ ("As if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night"): most readers read *qit'an* with a fatha on the *ṭā'*, the plural of *qit'ah*. In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهُمْ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا مَكانَكُمْ أَنْتُمْ وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ ("And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all; then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners'"): i.e., stand and remain in your places and do not move. The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

﴿وَقالَ شُرَكاؤُهُمْ ما كُنْتُمْ إِيَّانا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("And their partners will say: 'You did not used to worship us.'"): they will say, "Yes, you did worship us." Then the idols will say:

﴿فَكَفى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيداً بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنْ كُنَّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكُمْ لَغافِلِينَ﴾ ("Sufficient is Allah as witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship"): i.e., we were not aware of your worship of us, except that we were heedless, did not hear, did not see, and did not understand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿هُنالِكَ تَبْلُوا كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾ ("There, every soul will experience what it had sent forward"): *tabluw* means "it will test/inform," and it was also said: "it will know." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾: its record. It was also said: the meaning is that it follows what it sent forward of good and evil. Ibn Zayd said: [it is] "cooperates." ﴿وَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلاهُمُ الْحَقِّ﴾ ("And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master"); ﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ ("And what they used to invent will vanish from them"): i.e., the deities will perish [from them].

﴿قُلْ مَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ ("Say: 'Who provides for you from the sky'"): the rain; ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: the plants. ﴿أَمَّنْ يَمْلِكُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصارَ﴾ ("Or who controls hearing and sight?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ وَيُخْرِجُ الْمَيِّتَ مِنَ الْحَيِّ﴾ ("And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ ("And who arranges the affair?"). ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("They will say: 'Allah'"): the One who did these things. ﴿فَقُلْ أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Say: 'Will you not then fear [Him]?'"): i.e., will you not fear His punishment for your polytheism?

﴿فَذلِكُمُ اللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ الْحَقُّ﴾ ("Then that is Allah, your true Lord"): the One who does these things. ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الْحَقِّ إِلَّا الضَّلالُ فَأَنَّى تُصْرَفُونَ﴾ ("So what is there after the truth but error? Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

﴿كَذلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("Thus the word of your Lord has been justified"): al-Kalbi explained it as "thus," the same in all of the Qur'an. *Haqqat* means "became due"; *kalimat Rabbika* means His decree and His prior knowledge.

Al-A'raj read *kalimāt* ("words"). ﴿عَلَى الَّذِينَ فَسَقُوا﴾ ("upon those who defied"): i.e., disbelieved. ﴿أَنَّهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("that they will not believe").

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, the assimilated *yā'* changed to *hā'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. 'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

Yahya ibn Adam narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a kasrah on the *hā'* and the *yā'*, and a shaddah on the *dāl*, [to follow] the kasrah with the kasrah. It was also said: it is according to the dialect of those who read *na'budu* and *nasta'īnu*, and *lan tamassanā al-nār*, and similar words.

Abu 'Amr read between fatha and *jazm*, according to his method of *ikhfā'* (partial articulation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يُهْدى﴾ ("unless he is guided"): the meaning of the verse has two aspects. One group directed it to the leaders and the misguided ones: meaning, they do not guide unless they are guided. Others understood it as referring to the idols, and said: the sense of the expression is that it does not move unless it is carried and transported from its place, unless it is moved, as in the words of the poet:

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

﴿فَما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ﴾ ("What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهُمْ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا مَكانَكُمْ أَنْتُمْ وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ ("And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all; then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners'"): i.e., stand and remain in your places and do not move. The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

﴿وَقالَ شُرَكاؤُهُمْ ما كُنْتُمْ إِيَّانا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("And their partners will say: 'You did not used to worship us.'"): they will say, "Yes, you did worship us." Then the idols will say:

﴿فَكَفى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيداً بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنْ كُنَّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكُمْ لَغافِلِينَ﴾ ("Sufficient is Allah as witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship"): i.e., we were not aware of your worship of us, except that we were heedless, did not hear, did not see, and did not understand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿هُنالِكَ تَبْلُوا كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾ ("There, every soul will experience what it had sent forward"): *tabluw* means "it will test/inform," and it was also said: "it will know." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾: its record. It was also said: the meaning is that it follows what it sent forward of good and evil. Ibn Zayd said: [it is] "cooperates." ﴿وَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلاهُمُ الْحَقِّ﴾ ("And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master"); ﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ ("And what they used to invent will vanish from them"): i.e., the deities will perish [from them].

﴿قُلْ مَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ ("Say: 'Who provides for you from the sky'"): the rain; ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: the plants. ﴿أَمَّنْ يَمْلِكُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصارَ﴾ ("Or who controls hearing and sight?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ وَيُخْرِجُ الْمَيِّتَ مِنَ الْحَيِّ﴾ ("And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ ("And who arranges the affair?"). ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("They will say: 'Allah'"): the One who did these things. ﴿فَقُلْ أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Say: 'Will you not then fear [Him]?'"): i.e., will you not fear His punishment for your polytheism?

﴿فَذلِكُمُ اللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ الْحَقُّ﴾ ("Then that is Allah, your true Lord"): the One who does these things. ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الْحَقِّ إِلَّا الضَّلالُ فَأَنَّى تُصْرَفُونَ﴾ ("So what is there after the truth but error? Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

﴿كَذلِكَ حَقَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("Thus the word of your Lord has been justified"): al-Kalbi explained it as "thus," the same in all of the Qur'an. *Haqqat* means "became due"; *kalimat Rabbika* means His decree and His prior knowledge.

Al-A'raj read *kalimāt* ("words"). ﴿عَلَى الَّذِينَ فَسَقُوا﴾ ("upon those who defied"): i.e., disbelieved. ﴿أَنَّهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("that they will not believe").

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, the assimilated *yā'* changed to *hā'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. 'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

Yahya ibn Adam narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a kasrah on the *hā'* and the *yā'*, and a shaddah on the *dāl*, [to follow] the kasrah with the kasrah. It was also said: it is according to the dialect of those who read *na'budu* and *nasta'īnu*, and *lan tamassanā al-nār*, and similar words.

Abu 'Amr read between fatha and *jazm*, according to his method of *ikhfā'* (partial articulation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يُهْدى﴾ ("unless he is guided"): the meaning of the verse has two aspects. One group directed it to the leaders and the misguided ones: meaning, they do not guide unless they are guided. Others understood it as referring to the idols, and said: the sense of the expression is that it does not move unless it is carried and transported from its place, unless it is moved, as in the words of the poet:

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

﴿فَما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ﴾ ("What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

'Ata' narrated from him concerning ﴿هي﴾ (the reward): one good deed is counted as one, and *al-ziyadah* is the multiplication by ten of its like, up to seven hundred times. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/141–142.]]

Juwaybir narrated from al-Layth, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: *al-husna* is the (divine) look, and *al-ziyadah* is the gazing. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Mujahid said: *al-husna* is one good deed like one good deed, and *al-ziyadah* is ﴿مَغْفِرَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوانٌ﴾ ("forgiveness from Allah and approval"). Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

Mansur ibn 'Ammar narrated from Yazid ibn Shajarah, who said: *al-ziyadah* is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every kind of rare thing, and says to them: "What do you wish that I should rain upon you?" And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. Qatadah said: it is grief and gloom. Ibn Abi Layla said: this is after their looking at their Lord.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَنَّةِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").
