﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who originates creation'"): who creates from no prior source and no pattern. ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("then repeats it"): who brings it back to life in its form after death. [I.e., say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation.] [[Added from Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/341.]] ﴿فإن أجابوك﴾ ("If they answer you"): otherwise, say: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ فَأَنَّى تُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ ("Allah originates creation and then repeats it; so how are you deluded?"): i.e., turned away from the straight path.

﴿قُلْ هَلْ مِنْ شُرَكائِكُمْ مَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?'"): i.e., guides [others]. If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

The readers differed concerning this word. The people of Madina read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a *shaddah* on the *dāl*, because its origin is *yahtadī*: the *tā'* was assimilated into the *dāl*, and the *hā'* was left with a sukun in their reading, between two sukuns, as they did in ﴿تَعُدُّوا﴾ and ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, the assimilated *yā'* changed to *hā'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. 'Asim and Warsh read it with a kasrah on the *hā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl*, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. [Because when the *jazm* is forced to take a vowel, it changes to a kasrah.] Abu Hatim said: it is a dialect of Lower Mudar.

Yahya ibn Adam narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a kasrah on the *hā'* and the *yā'*, and a shaddah on the *dāl*, [to follow] the kasrah with the kasrah. It was also said: it is according to the dialect of those who read *na'budu* and *nasta'īnu*, and *lan tamassanā al-nār*, and similar words.

Abu 'Amr read between fatha and *jazm*, according to his method of *ikhfā'* (partial articulation). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *yahiddī* with a *jazm* on the *hā'* and a lightened *dāl*, in the sense of *yahtadī* ("is guided"). It is said: *hadaytuhu fa-hadā*, meaning *ihtadā* ("he was guided"). [Like:] *khabbartuhu fa-khabara* and *naqqaṣtuhu fa-naqaṣa*.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يُهْدى﴾ ("unless he is guided"): the meaning of the verse has two aspects. One group directed it to the leaders and the misguided ones: meaning, they do not guide unless they are guided. Others understood it as referring to the idols, and said: the sense of the expression is that it does not move unless it is carried and transported from its place, unless it is moved, as in the words of the poet:

*For the youth is an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot is guided.* [[The verse is by Tarafah, as in al-Sihah: 6/2534.]]

He means: wherever it is carried.

﴿فَما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ﴾ ("What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 10, verses 26–36:**

﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾ ("For those who did good is the best [reward] and more.")

Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Faqih informed us, along with others, who said: Abu 'Ali Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Saffar narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi narrated to me: Salm ibn Salm al-Balkhi narrated to me, from Nuh, from Ubayy, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى وَزِيادَةٌ﴾, and he said: "Those who did good deeds in this world: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is looking at the Noble Face of Allah."[79]

This is also the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), Hudhayfah, Abu Musa, Suhayb, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, 'Amir ibn Sa'd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The following supports it:

What Abu Ishaq ibn al-Fadl al-Qahandari informed us: Abu 'Ali al-Saffar informed us, al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit al-Bunani, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Suhayb, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will be called: 'O people of Paradise, indeed you have with Allah a promise that you have not seen.' They will say: 'And what is it? Did He not brighten our faces, distance us from the Fire, and admit us into Paradise?' Then the veil will be lifted—Blessed and Exalted is He—and they will look at Him." He said: "By Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than this."[80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/332.]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنى﴾ means those who testified that there is no god but Allah: Paradise.

'Ata' narrated from him concerning ﴿هي﴾ (the reward): one good deed is counted as one, and *al-ziyadah* is the multiplication by ten of its like, up to seven hundred times. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/141–142.]]

Juwaybir narrated from al-Layth, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: *al-husna* is the (divine) look, and *al-ziyadah* is the gazing. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ ناضِرَةٌ إِلى رَبِّها ناظِرَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.") [[Surah al-Qiyamah: 22–23.]]

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: *al-ziyadah* is a single chamber of pearl with four thousand doors.

Mujahid said: *al-husna* is one good deed like one good deed, and *al-ziyadah* is ﴿مَغْفِرَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوانٌ﴾ ("forgiveness from Allah and approval"). Ibn Zayd said: *al-husna* is Paradise, and *al-ziyadah* is what He gives them in response to their supplication, which He does not account against them on the Day of Resurrection.

Mansur ibn 'Ammar narrated from Yazid ibn Shajarah, who said: *al-ziyadah* is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every kind of rare thing, and says to them: "What do you wish that I should rain upon you?" And they wish for nothing except that it rains it upon them.

﴿وَلا يَرْهَقُ وُجُوهَهُمْ قَتَرٌ﴾ ("And neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces"): *yaghsha* means "covers and overtakes." *Qatar* means dust, and it is the plural of *qatarah*. The poet said:

*Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust.* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in al-Sihah: 2/785.]]

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is the blackness of the faces. Al-Hasan recited *qatr* with a sukun on the *ta'*, and both are dialectal forms, like *qadar* and *qadr*. ﴿وَلا ذِلَّةٌ﴾ means disgrace. Qatadah said: it is grief and gloom. Ibn Abi Layla said: this is after their looking at their Lord.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ الْجَنَّةِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَالَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ ("And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its like"): *jaza'* may be in the nominative by implying a prior element, meaning "for them is a recompense." It may also be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence whose predicate is *bi-mithlihā*, meaning "its like," with the *bā'* added to the predicate, as in their saying *bi-hasbika qawl al-su'* ("sufficient for you is the evil saying").

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ما لَهُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عاصِمٍ﴾ ("Humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah"): i.e., from the punishment of Allah; *min* here is for emphasis. "Protector" means one who prevents.

﴿كَأَنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعاً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِماً﴾ ("As if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night"): most readers read *qit'an* with a fatha on the *ṭā'*, the plural of *qit'ah*. In this reading, *muẓlliman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). *Qit'* (without *al-*) is in the accusative because the *alif* and *lam* were removed, as if he intended "a piece of the dark night." *Muẓlliman* may also be an adjective of *qit'* in the middle of the sentence, as in the poet's words: *law anna madḥata ḥayyin mansharā aḥadā*.

Abu Ja'far, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read *qiṭ'an* with a sukun on the *ṭā'*, and in that case *muẓlliman* is an adjective, in accordance with the verse ﴿بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("with a portion of the night"), and in agreement with the reading of Ubayy: *ka-annamā yughshā wujūhahum qiṭa'un min al-layl muẓlim*.

﴿أُولئِكَ أَصْحابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.")

﴿وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُهُمْ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا مَكانَكُمْ أَنْتُمْ وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ ("And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all; then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners'"): i.e., stand and remain in your places and do not move. The partners are the idols.

﴿فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("And We will separate them"): i.e., We will distinguish and divide between the polytheists and their partners, and sever the bonds of connection that existed between them in the world, when [they took] every object of worship besides Allah, from among His creation.

﴿وَقالَ شُرَكاؤُهُمْ ما كُنْتُمْ إِيَّانا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("And their partners will say: 'You did not used to worship us.'"): they will say, "Yes, you did worship us." Then the idols will say:

﴿فَكَفى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيداً بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَكُمْ إِنْ كُنَّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكُمْ لَغافِلِينَ﴾ ("Sufficient is Allah as witness between us and you; indeed we were unaware of your worship"): i.e., we were not aware of your worship of us, except that we were heedless, did not hear, did not see, and did not understand.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿هُنالِكَ تَبْلُوا كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾ ("There, every soul will experience what it had sent forward"): *tabluw* means "it will test/inform," and it was also said: "it will know." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, 'Isa, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tatlū* with a *tā'*, meaning "will follow/recite," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with the sense of "will read." [[That is, *tatlū* ("follows"); see Zad al-Masir: 4/25.]]

﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما أَسْلَفَتْ﴾: its record. It was also said: the meaning is that it follows what it sent forward of good and evil. Ibn Zayd said: [it is] "cooperates." ﴿وَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلاهُمُ الْحَقِّ﴾ ("And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master"); ﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ ("And what they used to invent will vanish from them"): i.e., the deities will perish [from them].

﴿قُلْ مَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ ("Say: 'Who provides for you from the sky'"): the rain; ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾: the plants. ﴿أَمَّنْ يَمْلِكُ السَّمْعَ وَالْأَبْصارَ﴾ ("Or who controls hearing and sight?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ وَيُخْرِجُ الْمَيِّتَ مِنَ الْحَيِّ﴾ ("And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living?"); ﴿وَمَنْ يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ﴾ ("And who arranges the affair?"). ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("They will say: 'Allah'"): the One who did these things. ﴿فَقُلْ أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Say: 'Will you not then fear [Him]?'"): i.e., will you not fear His punishment for your polytheism?

﴿فَذلِكُمُ اللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ الْحَقُّ﴾ ("Then that is Allah, your true Lord"): the One who does these things. ﴿فَماذا بَعْدَ الْحَقِّ إِلَّا الضَّلالُ فَأَنَّى تُصْرَفُونَ﴾ ("So what is there after the truth but error? Then how are you averted?"): i.e., from where are you turned away from His worship while you yourselves acknowledge it?

If they say "no," then they must concede it. ﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ يَهْدِي لِلْحَقِّ﴾ ("Say: 'Allah guides to the truth'"): i.e., to the truth. ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يُتَّبَعَ أَمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي﴾ ("Then is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not guide unless he is guided?").

He means: wherever it is carried.

How do you judge?"): i.e., you decide for yourselves. ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا﴾ ("And most of them follow nothing but assumption"): i.e., that they are deities and that they will intercede for them in the Hereafter. By "most" he meant all of them. ﴿إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئاً﴾ ("Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all"). ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do").

This is the Qur'an, which could not have been invented apart from God, but it is a confirmation of what came before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds. ﴿This Qur'an could not have been invented apart from God. Rather, it confirms what lies before it and details the Book, wherein there is no doubt from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "it is not fitting for this Qur'an to be invented," like His saying, ﴿It is not for a prophet to deceive﴾ and His saying, ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: "an" is in the accusative position as the predicate, and "yuftara" is its relative clause, and its implied meaning is: "this Qur'an was not invented." It was also said: "an" here has the meaning of "li" (in order to), so the meaning is: "the Qur'an was not such that it could be invented apart from God."

﴿...and a detailed explanation of the Book﴾ means distinguishing the lawful from the unlawful and the truth from falsehood. ﴿...in which there is no doubt from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

﴿Or do they say...?﴾ means: do they say.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "am" here means "wa" (and), so the meaning is: "and they say, 'he has invented it,' Muhammad fabricated the Qur'an on his own."

﴿Say: then bring a surah like it﴾, i.e., similar to the Qur'an. Ibn al-Sumayqa' read, "bi-surati mithlihi" with the word in the genitive construction, so the pronoun may refer to the Qur'an or to the Messenger. ﴿And call upon whomever you can﴾ from those you worship ﴿apart from God﴾ to help you in that. ﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾, i.e., among your people there will be those who will believe in the Qur'an. ﴿And among them are those who do not believe in it﴾, according to God's prior knowledge concerning them. ﴿And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters﴾, those who do not believe.

﴿And if they deny you﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿then say: "For me is my deed," the faith, ﴿and for you is your deed," the polytheism. ﴿You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do.﴾

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: this verse is abrogated (naskh, the repeal of a ruling by a later one) by the verse of jihad. Then He informed that success in belief in it comes only from Him and not from anyone else, and that no one believes except by His success and guidance. He mentioned that the disbelievers listen to the Qur'an and the words of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they look at him and see his signs and proofs of his prophethood, but these do not benefit them, nor are they guided, because of God's will and knowledge concerning them. It says: you cannot make hear the one whom God has deprived of hearing, nor can you create sight for the blind by which he may be guided. Likewise, you cannot grant them success in faith, since I have decided that they will not believe.

﴿Indeed, God does not wrong people at all﴾, because He is just in all His actions.

﴿But people wrong themselves﴾ through disbelief and disobedience, and through doing what is not theirs to do, [and He obligated them] to do what it is not for the doer to do.

﴿And the Day He gathers them, [it will be as if they had not remained] except an hour of the day﴾. Al-Dahhak said: ﴿as if they had not remained﴾ in the world except an hour of the day, meaning the world seemed short in their eyes because of the terror of what they faced. The exegetes said: some of what He showed him was at Badr, and the rest of the punishment came after their deaths.

﴿And for every nation there is a messenger. So when their messenger comes﴾ and they deny him, ﴿it will be judged between them with justice﴾, meaning they were punished in the world and destroyed justly and rightly.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: ﴿So when their messenger comes﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿it will be judged between him and them with justice, and they will not be wronged﴾, i.e., they will not be punished without sin, nor held accountable without proof, nor will their good deeds be diminished or their evil deeds increased.

I have no power over harm or benefit for them, ﴿except what God wills.﴾ ﴿For every nation is a term﴾, a time limit, [and a term], ﴿and when their term comes, [at the end] of their lives, ﴿they will not remain behind an hour, nor will they precede it.﴾ ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day, what is it that the criminals, the polytheists, would be hastening for?"﴾ and they have already fallen into it. ﴿Then—? Say: "Yes (*iy*), by my Lord, it is indeed true (*innahu la-haqq*), without any doubt about it, and you cannot escape (*wa-ma antum bi-mu'jizin*)," so be certain.

And if every soul that did wrong, that committed shirk, possessed everything on earth, it would surely ransom itself with it on the Day of Resurrection. They will conceal (*wa-asarru*), that is, hide, the regret for their disbelief when they see the punishment. The matter will be judged between them with justice (*bi-l-qist*), that is, their punishment will be finished, and they will not be wronged.

Indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true (*alā inna wa'da Allahi haqq*), up to His saying: "There has come to you an admonition (*mawi'zah*) from your Lord, a reminder (*tadhkirah*) and a healing (*shifa'*) and a cure (*diwa'*) for what is in the breasts," up to His saying, the Exalted: "Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy."

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: The grace of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made you among its people.

Ibn 'Umar said: The grace of Allah is Islam, and "His mercy" is its adornment in the heart.

Khalid ibn Ma'dan said: The grace of Allah is Islam, and "His mercy" is the Sunnah.

Al-Kisa'i said: The grace of Allah is the apparent blessings, and His mercy is the hidden blessings. Its proof is His saying: "And He has lavished upon you His blessings, apparent and hidden."

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: The grace of Allah is the bounties (*al-na'ma'*), which is what He gives and bestows, and His mercy is the favours (*al-ala'*), which is what He averts.

Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated: The grace of Allah is success (*al-tawfiq*), and His mercy is protection (*al-'isma*).

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: The grace of Allah is Islam, and His mercy is the Sunnah.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: The grace of Allah is faith (*al-iman*), and His mercy is Paradise.

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: The grace of Allah is entering the gardens (of Paradise), and His mercy is salvation from the Fire.

'Umar ibn 'Uthman al-Sadafi said: The grace of Allah is the lifting of the veil, and His mercy is the vision and the meeting (with Him).

Hilal ibn Yasaf, Mujahid and Qatadah said: The grace of Allah is faith, and His mercy is the Qur'an.

"So let them rejoice in that; it is better than what they accumulate," meaning the wealth. The majority of readers (*al-'ammah*) read both verbs with the *ya'* (third person, *fa-l-yafrahu*, *huwa khayrun mimma yajma'un*), as a report. Abu Ja'far read both with the *ta'* (second person), and this is attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Al-Husayn and Ya'qub read *fa-l-tafrahu* with the *ta'*, addressing the believers, and what supports this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in one of his campaigns: "Take your positions (*li-ta'khudhu mas-affakum*) [81] and gather (*wa-yajma'un*)."

With the *ya'*, it is a report about the disbelievers.

Say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers of Makkah: "Have you considered (*a-ra'aytum*) what Allah has sent down (*ma anzala Allah*), that is, created for you, expressing creation by 'sending down' because whatever good is in the earth from its produce descends from the sky, of provision (*min rizq*), that is, crops or livestock. Then you made from it what is forbidden (*haram*) and what is lawful (*halal*)," and this refers to what they forbade of the tilled land, the livestock, the *bahirah*, the *sa'ibah*, the *wasilah* and the *ha'mi*.

Al-Dahhak said: It is His saying: "And they assign to Allah a portion of what He has produced of the tilth and the cattle" [[Surah al-An'am: 136.]], the verse.

"Say: Did Allah permit you this forbidding and permitting, or do you invent (*am 'ala Allahi taftarun*) against Allah?" that is, their saying: "Allah commanded us with it." "And what will be the thought of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection?" Do they think that Allah will not call them to account or reproach them for it? "Indeed Allah is full of grace towards mankind," meaning He bestowed favour upon people by not hastening the punishment upon them for their fabrication, "but most of them do not give thanks."

"And you are not engaged in any affair (*sha'n*), that is, any work, and its plural is *shu'un*. Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs say, *ma sha'nuka sha'nuhu*, meaning, when you work at a work," "and you do not recite from it (*wa-ma tatlu minhu*), from Allah, any Qur'an," then He addressed him and his community together and said: "And you do not do any work, but We are witnesses over you when you engage in it (*idh tufidhuna fihi*)," that is, you take up and enter into it. The pronoun refers to the work. It is said: "Fulan *afada* in the speech and in the matter" when he excels in it.

Al-Ra'i said:

"And they poured forth after their silence in a flow, from Dhu al-Abariq, when they grazed the thick herb."

Ibn 'Abbas said: *Tufidhuna* means you do. Al-Hasan: you work. Al-Akhfash: you speak. Al-Mu'arrikh: you increase. Ibn Zayd: you conjecture. Ibn Kaysan: you spread abroad. It is said: "a widely spread report (*hadith mustafid*)." And it was said: you persist.

Al-Dahhak said: The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, meaning you listen in the Qur'an to falsehood.

It was said: Whoever witnesses the witnessing of the Truth definitively, that is through contemplation of all other than Him. "And not absent from your Lord" (*wa-ma ya'zubu 'an Rabbika*). Ibn 'Abbas said: "He is not absent (*fa-la yaghib*)." Abu Rawq said: "He is not far (*yab'ud*)." Ibn Kaysan said: "He does not depart (*yadhhab*)." [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/356.]]

Yahya, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read *ya'zibu* with a *kasrah* on the *zay*, and the rest read it with a *dammah*, and both are correct dialects (*lughatan [sahihatan]*). "Of an atom's weight" (*min mithqal*) is a complement: the meaning is, "And there is not absent from your Lord the weight of a dharrah or the weight of a dharrah," where the dharrah is the small red ant. The Arabs say: "[Take] this, for they are heavier in weight (*mithqal*) and lighter in weight (*mithqal*)," meaning in weight, "on earth or in heaven, nor anything smaller than that nor greater," which al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Yahya and Hamzah read with a *raf'* on the *ra'* in both places, in coordination with the position of *mithqal*, which justifies the entry of *min*. The rest read with a *fath* on the *ra'*, in coordination with *dharrah*, and "nor anything smaller than or greater than" (*wa-la asghara min dhalika wa-la akbara*), "except that it is in a Clear Book," meaning the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*).

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (*al-Jawahir al-Hisan*) on Surah 10, verses 62–70:

﴿Indeed, the allies of Allah—there shall be no fear concerning them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ Then He described them, saying: ﴿Those who believed and used to be mindful of Allah.﴾ Ibn Zayd said: "Faith will not be accepted except with taqwa (God-consciousness)." They differed over who deserves this title.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was asked about the allies of Allah, Exalted is He, and he said: "They are those whom, when seen, one remembers Allah." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/170.]]

'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said concerning this verse: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Among the servants of Allah are servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, yet the prophets and martyrs will envy them on the Day of Resurrection because of their standing with Allah." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell us who they are and what their deeds are, so that we may love them." He said: "They are a people who love one another for the sake of Allah, not because of kinship or wealth they exchange. By Allah, their faces are light, and they are upon pulpits of light. They do not fear when people fear, and they do not grieve when people grieve." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, the allies of Allah—there shall be no fear concerning them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ [82] [[al-Sihah: 3/1100.]]

'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The allies of Allah are a people whose faces are pale from vigil, whose eyes are sunken from weeping, whose bellies are empty from hunger [in Nahj al-Balagha and the tafsir of al-Qurtubi: hunger], whose lips are dry from thirst. [Al-dhawy: one who is not reached by moisture, or whom heat harms so that he wilts; it is said: adhwahu al-'atash (thirst withered him). In Ta'rikh Dimashq: from thirst (al-zama'); in Nahj al-Balagha: from supplication.]"

Ibn Kaysan said: "[They are those] whom Allah guided by the clear proof that came to them, and who took upon themselves the upholding of His right and the call to Him." ﴿For them is good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.﴾

On the authority of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿For them is good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.﴾ He said: "It is the righteous dream that a Muslim sees, or that is seen for him." [83]

And on the authority of 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abu al-Darda', that he was asked about this verse, ﴿For them is good tidings.﴾ He said: "You have asked about something I have not heard anyone ask about since I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one has asked me about it before you since revelation descended. It is the righteous dream that the believer sees, or that is seen for him; and in the Hereafter, it is Paradise." [84] [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/177; Musnad Ahmad: 6/445.]]

And on the authority of Yaman ibn 'Ubayd al-Rasibi, who said: Abu al-Tufayl 'Amir ibn Wathila narrated to us, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no prophethood after me, except the bearers of good tidings." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what are the bearers of good tidings?" He said: "The righteous dream." [85] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/454.]]

Muhammad ibn Sirin narrated from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the time draws near, the dream of a Muslim will hardly lie, and the most truthful of them in dreams are the most truthful of them in speech." He said: "Dreams are of three kinds: a dream of good tidings from Allah; a dream from what a man has been occupied with in his own soul; and a dream of grief from Satan. And a dream is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood. So if one of you sees something he dislikes, let him not recount it; let him stand and pray." He said: "I love the 'qayd' (fetter) in sleep and dislike the 'ghull' (shackle). The qayd is steadfastness in the religion." [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/507.]]

'Ubada ibn al-Samit said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, a man is loved by people for his deeds, yet he does not do the same deeds." He (ﷺ) said: "That is the hastened good tidings of the believer." [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/56.]]

Al-Zuhri and Qatada said: It is the good tidings the believer receives in this world at the time of death. Al-Dahhak said: It is that the believer knows where he will be before he dies. Al-Hasan said: It is what Allah has given them good tidings of in His Book—His Paradise and the generosity of His reward—in His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe﴾ [[Surah Yunus: 2.]] ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 223.]] ﴿and rejoice in Paradise﴾ [[Surah Fussilat: 30.]].

'Ata' said: ﴿For them is good tidings in the life of this world﴾: at death, the angels come to them with mercy and good tidings from Allah, while they come to the enemies of Allah with harshness and roughness; and in the Hereafter, at the moment the soul of the believer departs, it ascends to Allah just as a bride is escorted, being given glad tidings of Allah's pleasure. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are pure﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 32.]], to the end of the verse. Ibn Kaysan said: It is what Allah gave them good tidings of in this world through the Book and the Messenger: that they are the allies of Allah. And they are given good tidings in their graves and in their record, in which are their deeds, of Paradise.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿For them is good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾—the good praise. And he gestured with his hand.

﴿There is no alteration to the words of Allah﴾: no change to His word and no breaking of His promise.

Ibn 'Ulayya narrated from Ayyub, from Nafi', who said: Al-Hajjaj prolonged his sermon, so Ibn 'Umar placed his head on my lap. Al-Hajjaj said: "Ibn al-Zubayr altered the Book of Allah." Ibn 'Umar sat up and said: "Neither you nor Ibn al-Zubayr can alter ﴿the words of Allah﴾." Al-Hajjaj said: "You have shown forbearance [or: you have been given knowledge; that you would do so]." Ayyub said: When he turned to him privately, he fell silent. [[Addition from Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/181.]]

﴿That is the great triumph. And let not their speech grieve you﴾—meaning the speech of the polytheists. The statement is complete here.

Then He began anew: ﴿Indeed, all might [al-'izza, power] belongs to Allah﴾, and He is the One who takes vengeance upon them. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: ﴿Indeed, all might belongs to Allah﴾ means that Allah grants might to whom He wills, as He said in another verse: ﴿Might belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾; the might of the Messenger and the believers is from Allah, so it is all His. Allah said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe﴾ [[Surah al-Saffat: 180.]]. ﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And what do those who call upon other than Allah as partners follow?﴾ Here "ma" is interrogative: it says, "And what thing do those who call upon other than Allah as partners follow?" meaning they follow nothing, for they are not upon anything. The reading of al-Sulami is "tad'un" (with the ta'), meaning: what do your partners accomplish in the Hereafter? ﴿They follow only assumption﴾, meaning they assumed that these would intercede for them on the Day of Resurrection and bring them near to Allah in closeness; ﴿and they are only guessing.﴾

﴿He is the One who made for you the night that you may rest therein, and the day as something illuminating.﴾ That is: to be still, to be cool-eyed and to rest; "mubsiran" means illuminating, by which one sees. Like their saying: "a sleeping night," "a hidden secret," "a gushing water," and "a pleasing life." Jarir said:

*"Indeed, you blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, for traveling by night, and you slept, though the night of the camels is not sleeping."* [[Lisan al-'Arab: 2/2442; Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/183.]]

Qatrub said: The Arabs say: "The night became dark and the day shone, so one could see," meaning it became a thing of shade, light and sight.

﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who listen﴾ to admonitions, so that they may take heed. ﴿They say: Allah has taken a son.﴾ "They" means the polytheists, and this is their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. ﴿Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient; to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.⁠﴾ ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [i.e., you have no proof] and no evidence for this. You only named them, out of ignorance of them, an "authority" [and it is impossible] to hold to it. ﴿Do you say about Allah what you do not know?⁠﴾

﴿Say: Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will not succeed.﴾

Al-Kalbi said: "They will not believe." It is said: "They will not be saved." It is said: "They will not triumph." It is said: "They will not remain in this world." But it is a little enjoyment with which they take pleasure, and they benefit from it until the end of their term. "Mata'un" (enjoyment) is in the nominative by an implied supposition, meaning: for them is enjoyment; this is the view of al-Akhfash. Al-Kisa'i said: ﴿Enjoyment in this world﴾ [i.e., that is an enjoyment, or that is enjoyment]. ﴿Then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.⁠﴾

And recite to them (ﷺ), O Muhammad, to the people of Makkah, the news of Nuh (Noah) when he said to his people: ﴿O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then I have put my trust in God. So resolve upon your affair, you and your partners, and let not your affair be hidden from you. Then carry it out upon me and do not give me respite.﴾ Its meaning: if my staying among you and my admonishing you with the signs of God, that is, His proofs and clear evidences, is hard and heavy on you, and you resolve to kill me or drive me out, then ﴿I have put my trust in God﴾, that is, I have put my faith in God. ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾ is read by the majority of reciters with an alif at the beginning and a kasra on the mim (ajmi'u), meaning: prepare, firm up, and decide upon your affair, that is, resolve upon it.

The historian said: "ajma'tu al-amr" (I resolved upon the matter) is more eloquent than "ajma'tu 'alayhi" (I resolved upon it). He recited:

"Oh, if only I knew, though wishes do not help: Will I ever go out one day with my affair resolved?"

And al-A'raj and al-Jahdari read it as a connected verb with a fatha on the mim, from the root "jama'a", on the basis of His saying ﴿then he gathered his scheming﴾. Abu Mu'adh said: it may also mean "wa-ajma'u", that is, "fa-ajma'u" as one word; it is said "jama'tu" and "ajma'tu" with the same meaning.

Abu Dhu'ayb said: [he resolved upon it, as if he gathered himself for it, and the matter is gathered.]

As for ﴿and your partners﴾, there is an implied element in it, meaning: and call upon your partners, that is, your gods, and seek their help. Likewise in the codex of Ubayy it is: "and call upon your partners." Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Salam and Ya'qub read "wa-shurakā'ukum" in the nominative, meaning: resolve upon your affair, you and your partners together, that is, let your partners also gather with you. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the accusative for conformity with the written text, since there is no waw in it.

﴿Then let not your affair be hidden from you (ghummah)﴾, that is, obscure, dark, ambiguous and unclear, from their saying: "ghamma al-hilal 'ala al-nas" when it became unclear to them and they could not discern it. Tarafah said:

"By your life, my matter is not hidden from me: my day and my night are not hidden from me forever."

It is also said that it derives from "al-ghamm" (distress), because the chest becomes constricted, so the person cannot clearly see his matter, nor an opening from which what is in his heart may be relieved. Al-Khansa said:

"And one in distress, whose throat Ibn 'Amr had strangled, and whose face was covered, then it was uncovered."

﴿Then carry it out upon me﴾: that is, come forward with what is in your minds, or finish with it. It is said: "qada fulan" when he died and passed away, and "qada minhu" when he finished with it.

Al-Dahhak said: it means "rise up against me." Al-Farra' related from some reciters: "ifdu ilayya" with a fa', meaning: proceed until you reach me, as one says "anṣata al-khala'iq ila fulan" and "afḍa ila al-wajh." ﴿And do not give me respite﴾, that is, do not be given time.

This is a report from God, Exalted, about His Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him), that he was confident in the help of God and unafraid of the plots and calamities of his people, knowing that they and their gods neither benefit nor harm anything except what God wills, and it is a consolation to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and a strengthening of his heart.

﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, you turn away from my words and refuse to accept my counsel, ﴿then I have not asked you for any reward﴾, that is, wage or recompense, for the call and the delivery of the message. ﴿My reward is only upon God﴾: my recompense and my reward are only from God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾

﴿Then they denied him﴾, meaning Nuh. ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the ark, and We made them successors﴾, inhabitants of the earth, succeeding those who perished. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾, meaning [those who were humiliated] among those whom the messengers warned but who did not believe.

﴿Then after him﴾, that is, after Nuh, ﴿We sent messengers to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs﴾, with signs and commands and prohibitions, ﴿but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, meaning: they did not believe in what they had denied, and what they had denied before. ﴿Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors﴾, that is, the ones who exceed the lawful to the unlawful.

﴿Then after them﴾, that is, after Nuh, [Musa (Moses)] and [Harun (Aaron)] were sent ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, meaning the individuals of his people, ﴿with Our signs, but they were arrogant and they were a criminal people.﴾

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning Pharaoh and his people, they said: ﴿This is indeed clear magic.﴾ Musa said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, "Is this magic?" ﴾ The sense of the speech is: "Do you say of the truth when it came to you, 'magic'? Is this magic?" The first word "magic" is elided, and the meaning is indicated by what follows, like His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, to distress your faces﴾, meaning: to cover you so that they may distress your faces.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"When they wrapped the night, or when she was set up for him, and from her ears the [ornament] was leaning..."

That is: or when it [the night] approached. ﴿And the magicians do not prosper.﴾

They said, meaning Pharaoh and his people: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away, to twist us and divert us from what we found our fathers upon,﴾ from religion, ﴿and that greatness may be yours in the earth, in the land [of Egypt]? We are not believers in you two.﴾

Pharaoh said: ﴿Bring me every knowing magician.﴾ ﴿So when the magicians came, Musa said to them: "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So when they threw, Musa said: "What you have brought is magic"﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic.

The reading of Mujahid, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far is "ā-siḥr" with a madd, as an interrogative. The evidence for the majority reading is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "what you brought is magic," and the reading of Ubayy: "what you came with is magic." ﴿Indeed God will nullify it. Indeed God does not set right the work of the corrupters. And God will establish the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾

﴿But no one believed in Musa, except a offspring of his people﴾, that is, he did not believe in Musa despite whatever proofs he brought them. Some said: the pronoun returns to Musa, and by them he meant the believers of the Children of Israel.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they were six hundred thousand, because Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt with seventy-two persons, and they multiplied in Egypt until they reached six hundred thousand.

Mujahid said: he meant by them the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent among the Children of Israel, because of the length of time: the fathers perished and the sons remained. Others said: the pronoun returns to Pharaoh.

'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: they were a few people from the people of Pharaoh who believed, among them the wife of Pharaoh, the believer of the family of Pharaoh, the treasurer of Pharaoh, his treasurer's wife, and his hairdresser.

It was also related from Ibn 'Abbas by another route: they were seventy households of the Copts from the family of Pharaoh, whose mothers were from the Children of Israel, so a man would follow his mother and maternal uncles.

Al-Farra' said: they were called "dhurriyyah" because their fathers were Copts and their mothers were from the Children of Israel, as one says of the sons of the Persians who moved to Yemen that they are "al-abna'" (the sons), because their mothers are not of the same kind as their fathers. The "dhurriyyah" is the offspring, young and old, ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾, meaning the pronoun in "their people" refers to Pharaoh, and the pronoun in "their chiefs" refers back to the offspring; and whoever returns the pronoun to Musa, it means: the chiefs of Pharaoh.

Al-Farra' said: He said "their chiefs" in the plural though Pharaoh is singular, because when the king is mentioned, the thought goes to him and to his companions. This is from the category of omitting the qualifier (al-mudaf). Wahb ibn Munabbih mentioned [that it refers] to him and his band, as one says: "the caliph came," meaning he and those with him. It may also be that by Pharaoh he meant the family of Pharaoh, [as in His saying]: ﴿Ask the town﴾, and ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾; [that he would] ﴿turn them away from their religion﴾, and He did not say "yaftinu-hum" (they would tempt them), because He informed that Pharaoh and his people were in [error].

﴿Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land and indeed he was among the extravagant﴾ [those who exceed the limit in disobedience and disbelief], because he claimed lordship.

Musa said to the believers of his people: ﴿O my people, if you have believed in God, then upon Him rely, if you are Muslims.﴾ They said: ﴿Upon God we have relied.﴾

Then they supplicated and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people, and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.﴾ Abu Mijlaz said: "Our Lord, do not make Pharaoh and his people prevail over us, lest they see that they are better than us and so increase in transgression." 'Ata' said: "Do not give them power over us, lest they do evil and kill." Mujahid said: "Do not punish us by the hands of an [oppressive people], nor punish us with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished,' and do not give us power over them, lest they be tried."

﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother [We commanded both of them]: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses a qiblah."﴾ It is said: "tabawwa'a fulan li-nafsihi baytan" when someone took a house for himself [and al-mubawwa' is the dwelling, from which God's saying "bawwa'ahu Allah manzilan" derives], when he took it for himself.

﴿And make your houses a qiblah.﴾ Most of the commentators said: The Children of Israel used to pray only in their churches and synagogues, and they were visible; when Musa was sent, Pharaoh commanded that the mosques of the Children of Israel be destroyed, and he prevented them from prayer, so they were commanded to take mosques for themselves in which to pray, out of fear of Pharaoh. This is the view of Ibrahim, Ibn Zayd, al-Rabi', and it is so, and it is the report of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Mujahid and Khalaf said: [Musa said] to those with him from the people of Pharaoh: pray toward the great churches; so they were commanded to make their houses mosques facing the Ka'bah, and they would pray in them secretly. The meaning of "houses" here [is] the mosques.

The sense of the verse: "and make your houses toward the qiblah." This is the report of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Ka'bah was the qiblah of Musa and those with him." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: its meaning is: "make your houses face one another," and the qiblah is the direction.

﴿And establish the prayer, and give good tidings to the believers.﴾ O Muhammad.

Then carry it out upon me and do not give me respite.﴾ Its meaning: if my staying among you and my admonishing you with the signs of God, that is, His proofs and clear evidences, is hard and heavy on you, and you resolve to kill me or drive me out, then ﴿I have put my trust in God﴾, that is, I have put my faith in God. ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾ is read by the majority of reciters with an alif at the beginning and a kasra on the mim (ajmi'u), meaning: prepare, firm up, and decide upon your affair, that is, resolve upon it.

"Oh, if only I knew, though wishes do not help: Will I ever go out one day with my affair resolved?"

And al-A'raj and al-Jahdari read it as a connected verb with a fatha on the mim, from the root "jama'a", on the basis of His saying ﴿then he gathered his scheming﴾. Abu Mu'adh said: it may also mean "wa-ajma'u", that is, "fa-ajma'u" as one word; it is said "jama'tu" and "ajma'tu" with the same meaning.

Abu Dhu'ayb said: [he resolved upon it, as if he gathered himself for it, and the matter is gathered.]

As for ﴿and your partners﴾, there is an implied element in it, meaning: and call upon your partners, that is, your gods, and seek their help. Likewise in the codex of Ubayy it is: "and call upon your partners." Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Salam and Ya'qub read "wa-shurakā'ukum" in the nominative, meaning: resolve upon your affair, you and your partners together, that is, let your partners also gather with you. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the accusative for conformity with the written text, since there is no waw in it.

﴿Then let not your affair be hidden from you (ghummah)﴾, that is, obscure, dark, ambiguous and unclear, from their saying: "ghamma al-hilal 'ala al-nas" when it became unclear to them and they could not discern it. Tarafah said:

"By your life, my matter is not hidden from me: my day and my night are not hidden from me forever."

It is also said that it derives from "al-ghamm" (distress), because the chest becomes constricted, so the person cannot clearly see his matter, nor an opening from which what is in his heart may be relieved. Al-Khansa said:

"And one in distress, whose throat Ibn 'Amr had strangled, and whose face was covered, then it was uncovered."

﴿Then carry it out upon me﴾: that is, come forward with what is in your minds, or finish with it. It is said: "qada fulan" when he died and passed away, and "qada minhu" when he finished with it.

Al-Dahhak said: it means "rise up against me." Al-Farra' related from some reciters: "ifdu ilayya" with a fa', meaning: proceed until you reach me, as one says "anṣata al-khala'iq ila fulan" and "afḍa ila al-wajh." ﴿And do not give me respite﴾, that is, do not be given time.

This is a report from God, Exalted, about His Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him), that he was confident in the help of God and unafraid of the plots and calamities of his people, knowing that they and their gods neither benefit nor harm anything except what God wills, and it is a consolation to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and a strengthening of his heart.

﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, you turn away from my words and refuse to accept my counsel, ﴿then I have not asked you for any reward﴾, that is, wage or recompense, for the call and the delivery of the message. ﴿My reward is only upon God﴾: my recompense and my reward are only from God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾

﴿Then they denied him﴾, meaning Nuh. ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the ark, and We made them successors﴾, inhabitants of the earth, succeeding those who perished. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾, meaning [those who were humiliated] among those whom the messengers warned but who did not believe.

﴿Then after him﴾, that is, after Nuh, ﴿We sent messengers to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs﴾, with signs and commands and prohibitions, ﴿but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, meaning: they did not believe in what they had denied, and what they had denied before. ﴿Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors﴾, that is, the ones who exceed the lawful to the unlawful.

﴿Then after them﴾, that is, after Nuh, [Musa (Moses)] and [Harun (Aaron)] were sent ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, meaning the individuals of his people, ﴿with Our signs, but they were arrogant and they were a criminal people.﴾

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning Pharaoh and his people, they said: ﴿This is indeed clear magic.﴾ Musa said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, "Is this magic?" ﴾ The sense of the speech is: "Do you say of the truth when it came to you, 'magic'? Is this magic?" The first word "magic" is elided, and the meaning is indicated by what follows, like His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, to distress your faces﴾, meaning: to cover you so that they may distress your faces.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"When they wrapped the night, or when she was set up for him, and from her ears the [ornament] was leaning..."

That is: or when it [the night] approached. ﴿And the magicians do not prosper.﴾

They said, meaning Pharaoh and his people: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away, to twist us and divert us from what we found our fathers upon,﴾ from religion, ﴿and that greatness may be yours in the earth, in the land [of Egypt]? We are not believers in you two.﴾

Pharaoh said: ﴿Bring me every knowing magician.﴾ ﴿So when the magicians came, Musa said to them: "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So when they threw, Musa said: "What you have brought is magic"﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic.

The reading of Mujahid, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far is "ā-siḥr" with a madd, as an interrogative. The evidence for the majority reading is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "what you brought is magic," and the reading of Ubayy: "what you came with is magic." ﴿Indeed God will nullify it. Indeed God does not set right the work of the corrupters. And God will establish the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾

﴿But no one believed in Musa, except a offspring of his people﴾, that is, he did not believe in Musa despite whatever proofs he brought them. Some said: the pronoun returns to Musa, and by them he meant the believers of the Children of Israel.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they were six hundred thousand, because Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt with seventy-two persons, and they multiplied in Egypt until they reached six hundred thousand.

Mujahid said: he meant by them the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent among the Children of Israel, because of the length of time: the fathers perished and the sons remained. Others said: the pronoun returns to Pharaoh.

'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: they were a few people from the people of Pharaoh who believed, among them the wife of Pharaoh, the believer of the family of Pharaoh, the treasurer of Pharaoh, his treasurer's wife, and his hairdresser.

It was also related from Ibn 'Abbas by another route: they were seventy households of the Copts from the family of Pharaoh, whose mothers were from the Children of Israel, so a man would follow his mother and maternal uncles.

Al-Farra' said: they were called "dhurriyyah" because their fathers were Copts and their mothers were from the Children of Israel, as one says of the sons of the Persians who moved to Yemen that they are "al-abna'" (the sons), because their mothers are not of the same kind as their fathers. The "dhurriyyah" is the offspring, young and old, ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾, meaning the pronoun in "their people" refers to Pharaoh, and the pronoun in "their chiefs" refers back to the offspring; and whoever returns the pronoun to Musa, it means: the chiefs of Pharaoh.

This is from the category of omitting the qualifier (al-mudaf). Wahb ibn Munabbih mentioned [that it refers] to him and his band, as one says: "the caliph came," meaning he and those with him. It may also be that by Pharaoh he meant the family of Pharaoh, [as in His saying]: ﴿Ask the town﴾, and ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾; [that he would] ﴿turn them away from their religion﴾, and He did not say "yaftinu-hum" (they would tempt them), because He informed that Pharaoh and his people were in [error].

﴿Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land and indeed he was among the extravagant﴾ [those who exceed the limit in disobedience and disbelief], because he claimed lordship.

Musa said to the believers of his people: ﴿O my people, if you have believed in God, then upon Him rely, if you are Muslims.﴾ They said: ﴿Upon God we have relied.﴾

Then they supplicated and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people, and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.﴾ Abu Mijlaz said: "Our Lord, do not make Pharaoh and his people prevail over us, lest they see that they are better than us and so increase in transgression." 'Ata' said: "Do not give them power over us, lest they do evil and kill." Mujahid said: "Do not punish us by the hands of an [oppressive people], nor punish us with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished,' and do not give us power over them, lest they be tried."

'Ata' said: "Do not give them power over us, lest they do evil and kill." Mujahid said: "Do not punish us by the hands of an [oppressive people], nor punish us with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished,' and do not give us power over them, lest they be tried."

﴿And make your houses a qiblah.﴾ Most of the commentators said: The Children of Israel used to pray only in their churches and synagogues, and they were visible; when Musa was sent, Pharaoh commanded that the mosques of the Children of Israel be destroyed, and he prevented them from prayer, so they were commanded to take mosques for themselves in which to pray, out of fear of Pharaoh. This is the view of Ibrahim, Ibn Zayd, al-Rabi', and it is so, and it is the report of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Mujahid and Khalaf said: [Musa said] to those with him from the people of Pharaoh: pray toward the great churches; so they were commanded to make their houses mosques facing the Ka'bah, and they would pray in them secretly. The meaning of "houses" here [is] the mosques.

﴿And establish the prayer, and give good tidings to the believers.﴾ O Muhammad.

And recite to them (ﷺ), O Muhammad, to the people of Makkah, the news of Nuh (Noah) when he said to his people: ﴿O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then I have put my trust in God. So resolve upon your affair, you and your partners, and let not your affair be hidden from you. Then carry it out upon me and do not give me respite.﴾ Its meaning: if my staying among you and my admonishing you with the signs of God, that is, His proofs and clear evidences, is hard and heavy on you, and you resolve to kill me or drive me out, then ﴿I have put my trust in God﴾, that is, I have put my faith in God. ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾ is read by the majority of reciters with an alif at the beginning and a kasra on the mim (ajmi'u), meaning: prepare, firm up, and decide upon your affair, that is, resolve upon it.

"Oh, if only I knew, though wishes do not help: Will I ever go out one day with my affair resolved?"

And al-A'raj and al-Jahdari read it as a connected verb with a fatha on the mim, from the root "jama'a", on the basis of His saying ﴿then he gathered his scheming﴾. Abu Mu'adh said: it may also mean "wa-ajma'u", that is, "fa-ajma'u" as one word; it is said "jama'tu" and "ajma'tu" with the same meaning.

Abu Dhu'ayb said: [he resolved upon it, as if he gathered himself for it, and the matter is gathered.]

As for ﴿and your partners﴾, there is an implied element in it, meaning: and call upon your partners, that is, your gods, and seek their help. Likewise in the codex of Ubayy it is: "and call upon your partners." Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Salam and Ya'qub read "wa-shurakā'ukum" in the nominative, meaning: resolve upon your affair, you and your partners together, that is, let your partners also gather with you. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the accusative for conformity with the written text, since there is no waw in it.

﴿Then let not your affair be hidden from you (ghummah)﴾, that is, obscure, dark, ambiguous and unclear, from their saying: "ghamma al-hilal 'ala al-nas" when it became unclear to them and they could not discern it. Tarafah said:

"By your life, my matter is not hidden from me: my day and my night are not hidden from me forever."

It is also said that it derives from "al-ghamm" (distress), because the chest becomes constricted, so the person cannot clearly see his matter, nor an opening from which what is in his heart may be relieved. Al-Khansa said:

"And one in distress, whose throat Ibn 'Amr had strangled, and whose face was covered, then it was uncovered."

﴿Then carry it out upon me﴾: that is, come forward with what is in your minds, or finish with it. It is said: "qada fulan" when he died and passed away, and "qada minhu" when he finished with it.

Al-Dahhak said: it means "rise up against me." Al-Farra' related from some reciters: "ifdu ilayya" with a fa', meaning: proceed until you reach me, as one says "anṣata al-khala'iq ila fulan" and "afḍa ila al-wajh." ﴿And do not give me respite﴾, that is, do not be given time.

This is a report from God, Exalted, about His Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him), that he was confident in the help of God and unafraid of the plots and calamities of his people, knowing that they and their gods neither benefit nor harm anything except what God wills, and it is a consolation to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and a strengthening of his heart.

﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, you turn away from my words and refuse to accept my counsel, ﴿then I have not asked you for any reward﴾, that is, wage or recompense, for the call and the delivery of the message. ﴿My reward is only upon God﴾: my recompense and my reward are only from God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾

﴿Then they denied him﴾, meaning Nuh. ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the ark, and We made them successors﴾, inhabitants of the earth, succeeding those who perished. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾, meaning [those who were humiliated] among those whom the messengers warned but who did not believe.

﴿Then after him﴾, that is, after Nuh, ﴿We sent messengers to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs﴾, with signs and commands and prohibitions, ﴿but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, meaning: they did not believe in what they had denied, and what they had denied before. ﴿Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors﴾, that is, the ones who exceed the lawful to the unlawful.

﴿Then after them﴾, that is, after Nuh, [Musa (Moses)] and [Harun (Aaron)] were sent ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, meaning the individuals of his people, ﴿with Our signs, but they were arrogant and they were a criminal people.﴾

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning Pharaoh and his people, they said: ﴿This is indeed clear magic.﴾ Musa said: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, "Is this magic?" ﴾ The sense of the speech is: "Do you say of the truth when it came to you, 'magic'? Is this magic?" The first word "magic" is elided, and the meaning is indicated by what follows, like His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, to distress your faces﴾, meaning: to cover you so that they may distress your faces.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"When they wrapped the night, or when she was set up for him, and from her ears the [ornament] was leaning..."

That is: or when it [the night] approached. ﴿And the magicians do not prosper.﴾

The first word "magic" is elided, and the meaning is indicated by what follows, like His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, to distress your faces﴾, meaning: to cover you so that they may distress your faces.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"When they wrapped the night, or when she was set up for him, and from her ears the [ornament] was leaning..."

That is: or when it [the night] approached. ﴿And the magicians do not prosper.﴾

They said, meaning Pharaoh and his people: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away, to twist us and divert us from what we found our fathers upon,﴾ from religion, ﴿and that greatness may be yours in the earth, in the land [of Egypt]? We are not believers in you two.﴾

Pharaoh said: ﴿Bring me every knowing magician.﴾ ﴿So when the magicians came, Musa said to them: "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So when they threw, Musa said: "What you have brought is magic"﴾, that is, what you have brought is magic.

The reading of Mujahid, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far is "ā-siḥr" with a madd, as an interrogative. The evidence for the majority reading is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "what you brought is magic," and the reading of Ubayy: "what you came with is magic." ﴿Indeed God will nullify it. Indeed God does not set right the work of the corrupters. And God will establish the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾

﴿But no one believed in Musa, except a offspring of his people﴾, that is, he did not believe in Musa despite whatever proofs he brought them. Some said: the pronoun returns to Musa, and by them he meant the believers of the Children of Israel.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they were six hundred thousand, because Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt with seventy-two persons, and they multiplied in Egypt until they reached six hundred thousand.

Mujahid said: he meant by them the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent among the Children of Israel, because of the length of time: the fathers perished and the sons remained. Others said: the pronoun returns to Pharaoh.

'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: they were a few people from the people of Pharaoh who believed, among them the wife of Pharaoh, the believer of the family of Pharaoh, the treasurer of Pharaoh, his treasurer's wife, and his hairdresser.

It was also related from Ibn 'Abbas by another route: they were seventy households of the Copts from the family of Pharaoh, whose mothers were from the Children of Israel, so a man would follow his mother and maternal uncles.

Al-Farra' said: they were called "dhurriyyah" because their fathers were Copts and their mothers were from the Children of Israel, as one says of the sons of the Persians who moved to Yemen that they are "al-abna'" (the sons), because their mothers are not of the same kind as their fathers. The "dhurriyyah" is the offspring, young and old, ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾, meaning the pronoun in "their people" refers to Pharaoh, and the pronoun in "their chiefs" refers back to the offspring; and whoever returns the pronoun to Musa, it means: the chiefs of Pharaoh.

Al-Farra' said: He said "their chiefs" in the plural though Pharaoh is singular, because when the king is mentioned, the thought goes to him and to his companions. This is from the category of omitting the qualifier (al-mudaf). Wahb ibn Munabbih mentioned [that it refers] to him and his band, as one says: "the caliph came," meaning he and those with him. It may also be that by Pharaoh he meant the family of Pharaoh, [as in His saying]: ﴿Ask the town﴾, and ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾; [that he would] ﴿turn them away from their religion﴾, and He did not say "yaftinu-hum" (they would tempt them), because He informed that Pharaoh and his people were in [error].

﴿Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land and indeed he was among the extravagant﴾ [those who exceed the limit in disobedience and disbelief], because he claimed lordship.

Musa said to the believers of his people: ﴿O my people, if you have believed in God, then upon Him rely, if you are Muslims.﴾ They said: ﴿Upon God we have relied.﴾

Then they supplicated and said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people, and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.﴾ Abu Mijlaz said: "Our Lord, do not make Pharaoh and his people prevail over us, lest they see that they are better than us and so increase in transgression." 'Ata' said: "Do not give them power over us, lest they do evil and kill." Mujahid said: "Do not punish us by the hands of an [oppressive people], nor punish us with a punishment from You, lest the people of Pharaoh say: 'If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished,' and do not give us power over them, lest they be tried."

﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother [We commanded both of them]: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses a qiblah."﴾ It is said: "tabawwa'a fulan li-nafsihi baytan" when someone took a house for himself [and al-mubawwa' is the dwelling, from which God's saying "bawwa'ahu Allah manzilan" derives], when he took it for himself.

﴿And make your houses a qiblah.﴾ Most of the commentators said: The Children of Israel used to pray only in their churches and synagogues, and they were visible; when Musa was sent, Pharaoh commanded that the mosques of the Children of Israel be destroyed, and he prevented them from prayer, so they were commanded to take mosques for themselves in which to pray, out of fear of Pharaoh. This is the view of Ibrahim, Ibn Zayd, al-Rabi', and it is so, and it is the report of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Mujahid and Khalaf said: [Musa said] to those with him from the people of Pharaoh: pray toward the great churches; so they were commanded to make their houses mosques facing the Ka'bah, and they would pray in them secretly. The meaning of "houses" here [is] the mosques.

The sense of the verse: "and make your houses toward the qiblah." This is the report of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Ka'bah was the qiblah of Musa and those with him." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: its meaning is: "make your houses face one another," and the qiblah is the direction.

﴿And establish the prayer, and give good tidings to the believers.﴾ O Muhammad.

Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way." Muqatil said: "adornment" means a fine appearance, as in His words: ﴿So he went out before his people in his adornment﴾.

Scholars differed concerning this lam (al-lam). Some said it is the lam of purpose (lam al-kay), and the meaning is: "You gave them so that they might go astray, become insolent and arrogant," in order to test them with it, so that they would go astray and lead others astray, as a respite from You. This is like His words: ﴿Had they remained upon the way, We would surely have given them abundant water, that We might test them therein﴾. It was also said: it is the lam of consequence and outcome (lam al-'aqibah wa al-sayrurah), meaning: He gave them so that they would go astray [......] [[blank in the manuscript.]] the people of Pharaoh, ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾. It was also said: it is a lam of cause, meaning: "We gave them because of their misguidance, as a punishment for them," like His words: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them﴾, meaning because of your turning away from them; they did not swear so that you would turn away from them.

﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾. ʿAtiyyah and Mujahid said: "Destroy it." Al-tams means erasing and effacing. Most of the exegetes said: "Transform it and change it from its form." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "He made their coins stones." Qatadah said: "We have been told that their crops turned into stones." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The dirhams and dinars turned into stones, bearing the same engravings as they had, whole, and halves and thirds." Ibn Zayd said: "Their gold turned into stones, and their silver, lentils, and everything." Al-Suddi said: "God transformed their wealth into stones: the palm trees, fruits, flour and food, and this was one of the nine signs."

﴿And harden their hearts﴾, meaning: seal them so that they will not soften and will not open to faith.

﴿So they will not believe﴾. It was said: it is in the subjunctive as an answer to the supplication introduced by the fa' (fa' al-jawab). It was also said: it is coordinated with His words: [li-yudilloo] ("that they may lead astray").

Al-Farra' said: "It is a supplication, and its position is jussive, as if he said: O Allah, so let them not believe." It was also said: its meaning is "so let them not believe."

He said: ﴿Your supplication has been answered﴾, as a report from Allah the Exalted. [Ali and al-Sulami read "da'watukuma" in the plural, and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read: "qad ujibat da'watukuma" ("your supplication has been answered").]

Like the saying of al-A'sha:
"I said to my companion, do not hasten us
in pulling up its roots and cutting off the shih."

﴿So go straight on, following the message and the call, and proceed according to My command until the punishment of Allah comes to them.﴾

Ibn Jurayj said: "Pharaoh remained forty years after this supplication."

﴿And do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾. The prohibition here uses the heavy nun (nun al-tawkid al-thaqilah) and is in the jussive position. In the singular one says "la tattabi'anna," with the nun vocalized with fatha because of the meeting of two sukun, and in the dual it is vocalized with kasra for this same reason. Ibn ʿAmir read with the light nun, because the nun of emphasis may be heavy or light.

The meaning: "Do not take the path of those who ignore the truth of My promise, so that you hasten My decree; for My decree and My promise cannot be broken, and My threat is about to fall upon Pharaoh and his people."

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾, the verse. The reason: Allah the Exalted commanded Moses (peace be upon him) to take the Children of Israel out of Egypt, and the Children of Israel were among the Copts [so he brought them out] under the pretext of a wedding feast for them, and Moses traveled with them, they being six hundred thousand and twenty thousand, in which no one younger than seventy or twenty years old was counted [to the sea, and said to them] [[as in the original.]] the Copts that night, and they followed the Children of Israel until morning, and this is His words:

﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾, after they had buried their children. When Pharaoh reached [the sea], he rode with a million and six hundred thousand.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "In Pharaoh's army were a hundred thousand black stallions besides the other horses, and [........] [[blank in the manuscript.]] Harun was at the front of the Children of Israel and Musa at the rear. When they reached the sea and the vanguard of Pharaoh drew near them, a hundred thousand men, each with his head covered by a helmet and a spear in his hand, with Pharaoh behind them on a dumm (a wide-bodied mount). The Children of Israel said to Moses: 'Where is what you promised us? The sea is before us; if we cross it we drown, and Pharaoh is behind us; if he catches us, we are killed.' ﴿We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us.﴾

Then Moses said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and see how you act﴾, and he said: ﴿No indeed! My Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. Then Allah revealed to him: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff﴾, and he struck it, but it did not split. He said: "I am more forward than you and stronger in creation." Allah the Exalted then revealed to Moses: "Be quiet, and say: 'Split, O Abu Khalid, by the permission of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.'" He did so, and the sea split and became twelve paths, one for each tribe. Allah uncovered the face of the earth, and it became dry, and between every two paths a mountain rose.

They were cousins who could not see one another or hear one another's speech, so each group said: "Our companions have drowned." Allah the Exalted revealed to the mountains in the water: "Be interlaced," and they interlaced and became like openings in it, so that they could see one another.

When Pharaoh arrived with his armies at the sea and saw the sea in that state, Pharaoh said: "The sea has frightened me," and they feared entering the sea. Pharaoh was on a black stallion, and there was no mare among Pharaoh's horses. Gabriel came on a mare in heat [wadiq: one that desires the stallion], entered the sea, and Michael drove them, so no man strayed from them without his being joined to them.

When Pharaoh's black stallion smelled the scent of Gabriel's mare, and Pharaoh could not see it, it slipped after Gabriel's mare, and Pharaoh had no control over his affair at all. The horses plunged into the water, and when the last of them entered the sea and the first wished to come out, the water closed over them. When Pharaoh faced drowning he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims﴾. Gabriel said: ﴿Now? And you disobeyed before and were among the corrupters.﴾

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Allah said to Moses and Harun: ﴿Speak to him gently, that perhaps he may remember or fear﴾, when his remembrance and fear would no longer benefit him.

Ka'b said: When the Nile of Egypt stopped flowing, the Copts said to Pharaoh: "If you are our lord, make the water flow for us." He mounted and ordered his troops to mount. His herald would call every hour: "Let so-and-so stand with his troops, commander by commander." They stood upon their ranks until only he and his close attendants remained. He ordered them to stand, until only his chamberlains and servants remained; he ordered them to stand, and advanced alone, out of their sight, [and dismounted from his mount], and put on other garments, prostrated, and humbled himself before Allah. Allah made the water flow for him. Then Gabriel came to him alone in the form of a questioner and said: "What does the commander say about a man who has a slave who grew up in his blessings, having no master but him, who then denied his blessings, rejected his right, and claimed sovereignty over him?" [Pharaoh wrote: "His recompense is that he be drowned in the sea."] [[addition from al-Qurtubi's tafsir.]]

When Moses informed his people of the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, the Children of Israel said: "Pharaoh did not die and will never die." So Allah commanded the sea, and it threw Pharaoh onto the shore, a red, short creature like a bull. The Children of Israel saw him, and then the sea [they crossed it]. Al-Hasan read "wa-jawwaznā" (both are dialects of the same meaning).

﴿So Pharaoh pursued them﴾, that is, caught up with them. It is said: "tabi'ahu" and "atba'ahu" when one catches up with and overtakes someone, while "ittaba'ahu" with doubled ta' means he went behind him [and imitated him]. ﴿Pharaoh and his armies.﴾

﴿Out of insolence and enmity﴾: zulm (injustice) and transgression. It is said: 'ada ya'dū 'adwan, like ghazā yaghzū ghazwan. Al-Hasan read ('udūwan) with a damma on the ayn and shadda on the waw, like 'alā ya'lū 'ulūwan. The exegetes said: "bagyan" refers to speech and "'adwan" to action.

﴿Until, when drowning overtook him﴾, meaning it encompassed him. ﴿He said: "I believe that..."﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "innahu" with a kasra, meaning "I believe, and I said: 'indeed'," and this is the reading of Abdullah. The others read "annahu" with a fatha, because "āmantu" governs it; this is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

﴿There is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims.﴾ Gabriel said: ﴿Now? And you disobeyed before, and you were among the corrupters.﴾

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Gabriel said to me: 'I have never hated any of Allah's servants except that I hated two servants: one of the jinn and the other of mankind. As for the one of the jinn, it is Iblis when he refused to prostrate to Adam; as for the one of mankind, it is Pharaoh when he said: ﴿I am your highest lord﴾. And if you had seen me, O Muhammad, putting the mud into his mouth, for fear that mercy would reach him.'" [86] [[al-Tabari's Jami' al-Bayan: 19/102, with slight variation.]]

﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾, meaning We will place you on a raised place of the earth, and this is the najw, the high place. Aws ibn Hajar said:
"He who is in his high place is like one who is in his najwah,
and the one who hides is like one who walks in the open."

﴿In your body﴾: in your flesh without spirit in you. Mujahid and al-Kisa'i said: "Badan" here means armour, and he was wearing armour. Al-A'sha said:
"A fair one like a bright stream, woven, with a helmet above the front of the coat of mail."

Abdullah read: ﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾, meaning We will cast you upon the shore of the sea. It was also said: "your hair."

﴿That you may be a sign for those after you﴾: a lesson and admonition.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "li-man khalaqaka" with a qaf, meaning: that you may be a sign for your Creator.

﴿And indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs.﴾ Muqatil said: this means the people of Mecca. Al-Hasan said: it is general.

﴿Of Our signs﴾, that is, concerning faith in Our signs, [they are] heedless.
